item.content:encoded:
There was the 1-0 loss to the Guardians. There were the weather updates that might very well have the Red Sox and Cubs playing somewhere other than Fenway Park this weekend. And there was Ceddanne Rafaela's return from his hamstring scare.
But when it came to news that mattered for the Red Sox, it was hard to top what Willson Contreras said after this latest defeat.
The first baseman's bruised right hand evidently does not seem to be cooperating when it comes to postseason readiness.
"I mean, it's really concerning,” Contreras said. “But at the same time, I'm putting all my effort -- and everything I can do, I'm doing it. I don't know what else to say. I’m working hard with the trainers; the hand is slowly getting better. But I haven’t been able to swing the last two days. I’ll be honest with the team. I know Tuesday is a really important game. It's a really important series, and I'll be completely honest with the team.”
Contreras added, "It's frustrating, if I’m being honest. I was hoping to swing today, and I couldn't swing. I came into my locker just tearing up because that's what we play for. We play to play in October, and it's really frustrating when we're doing the best you can do and you're expecting to heal faster and that doesn't happen."
It appeared as though Contreras was headed in the right direction, taking an exorbitant amount of swings prior to Tuesday's game, both on the Fenway field and underneath with the Trajekt pitching machine. But the results from the exercise were not positive, with the righty hitter unable to replicate any sort of batting practice over the last couple of days.
There is still time for Contreras, with the Red Sox's first wild-card game on Tuesday. But his original plan to use the weekend games against the Cubs as a tune-up for the playoffs seems extremely unlikely.
Why is this such a big deal? It's because of the skill-set Contreras carries, one that the Red Sox seem starved for heading into the postseason.
All good postseason runs are usually built on the back of top-of-the-order power, with opponents needing to navigate their way through a team's alpha batters. Hitting home runs, in particular, is usually a top priority. The Blue Jays and Dodgers lived that life a year ago, as did the Yankees and Los Angeles the year before. You know who didn't? The 2025 Red Sox during their three wild-card games at Yankee Stadium.
Trevor Story's solo homer in Game 2 of last season's playoff showdown with the Yankees marked the only time a Red Sox player cleared the fences. It was a deficiency that was difficult to ignore.
It was why Craig Breslow proclaimed early in the offseason that his team needed more power. It was the reason acquiring Curtis Mead became a priority heading into the trade deadline. And it is why Contreras, who leads the Red Sox with 27 homers, has been so important. (The Red Sox are 18-8 when Contreras hits at least one homer.)
While this Red Sox team has taught us that things can turn in a hurry, the way the Sox's offense has been trending isn't good. In the last five games, the Sox have hit only two home runs. And in September, Chad Tracy's team has the second-lowest batting average and OPS in baseball, while scoring the fewest runs (13 fewer than the next-worst).
There are potential solutions to the Red Sox's postseason power problem, including Roman Anthony (who is tied with Mickey Gasper for the team lead in homers for September with four), Adley Rutschman, Story, Rafaela and Wilyer Abreu, who has two home runs since Aug. 16.
But Contreras has always been the constant ... until now.
“When it hurts, it hurts. Especially when it's the top hand,” Contreras said. “If it was the bottom hand, I could swing with the right hand, but when it's the right hand, my right hand just feels weaker until I just let the bat go. It's not a good sign. ... Again, I'm doing everything that I can to come back and play with the boys and be there with the boys. But sometimes you have to listen to your body, and I'm listening to the trainers and doing everything that they ask me to do, and [it's] just one of those things that I can't control."

item.content:encoded:
Rather than forcing fans to sit through a tense postseason run with an interim manager, the Boston Red Sox ripped the band-aid off and made one of the most obvious announcements of the season: Chad Tracy has earned the full-time manager job. The team and coach have agreed to a three-year extension that runs through 2029 with an option for the 2030 campaign.
It's a well-earned title, one which should take some pressure off Tracy ahead of his first foray into the postseason. Yet, as great as he's been, it's hard not to shake the feeling that this decision was as much about him as it was the coaching market.
By no means am I suggesting Tracy earned this job by default; this team was 32-46 just three months ago and then clinched a playoff spot with one week left to go in the regular season. Guiding the Red Sox out of that dark place into immediate success (they went 32-5 over their next 37 games) was nothing short of miraculous.
Rather, the point I'm trying to make is that Tracy was the only reasonable option for the Red Sox to go with. Just take a look at the best managerial candidates that are out there — none of them fit what this team needs moving forward.
Red Sox should be thankful Chad Tracy left them with no other choice for manager job
The clear-cut best option is Alex Cora, but considering Craig Breslow was also effectively extended (he had two years worth of options exercised), he was never returning to Boston. The odds are quite strong that he'll head to Philadelphia to take over for Don Mattingly, which means that competition for the other best candidates will be fierce this offseason.
Those include some retread hires like old friends David Ross and Rocco Baldelli, plus old enemy Brandon Hyde. The latter two in that group won Manager of the Year awards at their previous stops, but none of the trio are particularly inspiring. Baldelli is the only one with a record better than .500 as a skipper, and they've all combined for one playoff series win in 18 years.
Then there's the coaches looking for their first manager gig, including the likes of Carlos Beltrán and Albert Pujols. As exciting as it would have been to hire a Hall of Famer, moving on from Tracy just to hire another first-timer would have been a nonstarter. The biggest hole in his résumé is his lack of experience at the MLB level.
He's picked up some valuable experience this year, though, and the Red Sox are clearly better for it. Maybe this conversation would have been different if they never recovered from their first-half slump, but it's become clear over the past few months that Tracy really is the only man for the job.

item.content:encoded:
Many of us believe he’s the best pitcher we’ve ever seen. He’s a blue-chip, first-ballot Hall of Famer, part of the Red Sox team that broke the Curse, and seen on TBS after Sox playoff games in any given October. He’ll be 55 next month and spends every year shuttling between Boston and his native Dominican Republic, when he’s not working in Atlanta. He has no regrets about saying “The Yankees are my daddy,” all those years ago, and he thinks the Red Sox have a shot to beat the Yankees in New York next week.
He is the one and only Pedro Martinez, and he’s spending Thursday in Lawrence with his wife, Carolina, launching an after-school coding program at South Lawrence East Elementary School, then engaging in a question-and-answer session with hundreds of students at Lawrence High School.
“Lawrence has been kind of forgotten a little bit,” said Martinez. “It has gotten kind of old in front of our eyes, but there is so much need. If there’s something I can really identify myself with, it is need. I grew up in those kind of needs. I’m just expressing the cry I had when I was a kid. I get excited every time I see a kid that has an opportunity to become someone.”
Martinez’s new program is designed to bridge resource gaps and enhance classroom learning for young students across Lawrence. His foundation, dedicated to transforming the lives of youth in the United States and the Dominican Republic, was started in 1998 when he joined the Sox after five-plus stellar seasons with the Dodgers and Expos.
“I got a very pleasant surprise when I got to Fenway as soon as I saw the drums and the people with the [Dominican] flag and the atmosphere kind of changing,” Martinez recalled. “Mayor [Thomas] Menino was kind enough to take me in his SUV to give me a tour around Boston, and right away I fell in love with the people … and the Latino community all over the place, and that’s when I landed in Lawrence, Lynn, Dorchester, and all those areas that continue to be linked to me.”
It was in those early Boston days that Martinez’s Fenway mound starts “became the curfew back home in the Dominican every time I pitched.”
A connection was made; an ongoing, lasting relationship because of the Pedro Martinez Foundation.
In 2026, Martinez and teammate/countryman David Ortiz are listed as “special assistants” in the fourth line of the the Red Sox’ official front office directory, just below chief baseball officer Craig Breslow. Martinez occasionally helps young Sox pitchers at spring training, but he was out of the loop when the decision was made to fire manager Alex Cora and six coaches just 27 games into the season.
“I was actually talking to Alex a couple of days before,” Martinez remembered. “When I found out, I wasn’t angry, I just couldn’t understand how everything snowballed to that point.”
Martinez’s beloved former teammate, catcher/captain Jason Varitek, was part of the purge. The Sox claimed Varitek was “reassigned,” but he hasn’t surfaced anywhere in the organization.
Does Martinez think the burned bridge will be repaired?
“I think it’s going to be OK with Jason,” said the three-time Cy Young Award winner. “Jason is a very professional person. He understands that business part, just like Alex Cora.”
What does Martinez think about the local demonization of Rafael Devers?
“This is a very misunderstood kid,” he said. “Devers is very shy. But he is legit. He’s a guy that doesn’t know how to express himself and has a hard time trusting anybody but his father. His father knows the actual truth … Devers is very respectful, a very lovely kid, but now it’s over and the team is on its way to success. … You have to learn to love Boston if you want to survive in Boston. Boston is 24/7 talking about their sports.”
Does Martinez want Payton Tolle or Sonny Gray starting Game 1?
“You don’t go wrong with either one,” he said. “Sonny is a true professional, a true competitor. I love, love Tolle. Just his amazing attitude. I love every single pitch he throws. I love everything about him.
“The Yankees are vulnerable, especially without [Aaron] Judge. I don’t think the Red Sox are intimidated by the Yankees. I think they can beat not only the Yankees but any team in baseball.”
The highlight of Martinez’s baseball career?
“Being part of the 25 that brought the trophy to Boston.”
Ever wish he never said, “The Yankees are my daddy”?
“No. I was being honest. That’s what you guys demand from all of us. The Yankees had my number at that point, and I expressed it. I will tell you in the most honest way, I got my ass kicked.”
Which brings us back to 2003, when Grady Little was fired (almost immediately) after failing to take Martinez out of the game when Pedro was past his pitch limit after seven innings of Game 7 of the ALCS at Yankee Stadium. Martinez had fanned Alfonso Soriano on his final pitch of the seventh, was at 100 pitches, and believed he was done for the night.
“[Red Sox pitching coach] Dave Wallace told me I was done after, so I didn’t put my jacket on,” said Martinez. “I had looked up in the sky and gave thanks to God for the seven innings I pitched. Our bullpen was lights out. All of a sudden Grady was like, ‘I don’t like [Alan] Embree against Nick Johnson in the eighth.’ He said, ‘You give me Nick Johnson and I got the rest of the bullpen for you.’ That’s the true story.”
Back on the mound, leading, 5-2, in the eighth, Martinez retired Johnson on a second-pitch popup to start the inning, then looked to the dugout. Nobody moved.
“Nothing happened,” recalled Martinez. “So I just kept going. I gave up a couple of line drives, and everything just snowballed after that. I thought I made a great pitch on [Jorge] Posada, but Posada blooped it [for a two-run double].”
All in all, it was four straight hits and a tie game before Little finally pulled Martinez after 23 disastrous eighth-inning pitches. Then Aaron Boone (now the Yankees’ manager) happened in the 11th.
Two summers ago, Maryland congressman Jamie Raskin wrote President Joe Biden a letter, imploring America’s tiring leader to end his reelection campaign. As part of his logic, Raskin compared Biden’s career to Martinez’s Game 7 performance, writing that there is “no shame in taking a well-deserved bow … when your arm is tired out.”
Days later, Biden pulled out of the race.
“I don’t know what to tell you about that,” chuckled Martinez. “Grady just told me, ‘Get one more out.’ That was Nick Johnson, right?”
Right.
All these years later, the wounds have healed and Martinez is on a greater mission, taking his message to Lawrence.
“I don’t have enough words to describe how grateful I am to have my opportunity through baseball and make a difference now,” said Martinez. “My message to these kids in Lawrence is that nothing in life is too far away if you have the will, if you have the passion.”
Dan Shaughnessy is a Globe columnist. He can be reached at daniel.shaughnessy@globe.com. Follow him @dan_shaughnessy.

item.content:encoded:
Since being tapped as interim manager, Andy Green remained adamant he did not want the job long-term. Well, something changed and, now, the former Chicago Cubs bench coach is the man in Queens after signing a three-year extension that was announced on Tuesday.
It's been the better part of a decade since Green last managed. Prior to serving as Cubs bench coach, he was the skipper of the San Diego Padres from 2016-2019. After being fired in Sept. 2019, he came to Chicago as the right-hand man for first-time manager David Ross, who took over following the departure of Joe Maddon.
Baseball often has a funny way of bringing things full circle and with the interim tag coming off Green, Ross is among those who directly felt the impact of the move. The beloved former big-league backstop hasn't coached or managed since the Cubs dumped him for Craig Counsell prior to the 2024 campaign, but remains a logical candidate for any vacancy that opens.
Unfortunately for him, that list of potential opportunities just shrank by one as Green, who has thrived both in the clubhouse and with the media this year since stepping in for the fired Carlos Mendoza, takes another bite as an MLB manager.
David Ross could still see opportunities to get a new managerial gig
Crossing the Mets' job off the list, let's take a spin around the league to see which other managers could be on the outs. Really, it boils down to three (maybe four) gigs after Craig Breslow and Chad Tracy got some long-term certainty in Boston: Houston, Seattle, Arizona and, potentially, Philadelphia.
It feels like a foregone conclusion that the Astros, Mariners and Diamondbacks will be looking for new managers at season's end. Joe Espada, Dan Wilson and Torey Lovullo are all aware of that fact and, given the fact that none of those teams seem particularly likely to embark on immediate teardowns, they could seek a manager with some experience (enter Ross).
He'll face some stiff competition. The field of candidates include a pair of Hall of Famers in Albert Pujols and Carlos Beltran and a former World Series champion in the dugout in Alex Cora. That doesn't even take into account the dark horse candidates that always pop into these conversations.
That all being said, this partnership between Green and the Mets seems like a win-win for everyone involved... unless you're David Ross.

item.content:encoded:
보스턴 레드삭스는 22일(미국 현지시간) 단 한 번의 과감한 조치로 프런트오피스와 감독실 모두에 탄탄한 기반 안정을 구축했습니다.
보스턴 레드삭스 구단 역사상 손꼽히는 시즌 중반 대반전을 이끌어낸 채드 트레이시는 임시 감독 꼬리표를 떼어냈습니다. 이에 따라 지난 20일에 포스트시즌 진출을 확정 지은 트레이시는 2030년 팀 옵션이 포함된 2029시즌까지의 3년 계약에 합의하며 구단 역사상 제49대 감독으로 공식 취임했습니다.
한편, 2023년 가을 보스턴의 야구 운영 부사장(CBO)으로 부임한 크레이그 브레슬로우는 2029년과 2030년 계약 옵션을 행사하기로 했습니다.
샘 케네디 레드삭스 사장 겸 최고경영자(CEO)는 "오늘은 보스턴 레드삭스 구단에 매우 훌륭한 날입니다"라며, "오늘 전해진 소식보다 더 기쁠 수는 없습니다. 올 시즌 다사다난한 롤러코스터 같은 시간을 보냈는데, 이러한 발표를 하게 되어 정말 기쁩니다"라고 소감을 밝혔습니다.
이번 인사는 시즌 초반 32승 46패라는 부진한 출발을 보이며 험난했던 처음 3개월을 보낸 레드삭스가 어떻게 팀을 다시 안정궤도에 올렸는지를 보여주는 또 하나의 사례였습니다.
상황이 그토록 심각해지기 전, 브레슬로우는 10승 17패로 시즌을 시작한 직후 오랜 기간 팀을 이끌었던 알렉스 코라 감독과 코치 5명을 경질하며 과감하게 결단을 내렸습니다.
케네디 사장은 "두 사람이 가장 공통으로 갖고 있는 점은, 적어도 최근 들어 레드삭스가 두 사람 모두에게 매우 어려운 임무를 맡겼다는 사실입니다"라며, "브레슬로우, 당신은 2023년에 레드삭스의 야구 운영 부문을 지속적인 성공의 길로 이끌고, 월드시리즈 우승을 위해 경쟁할 수 있는 위치로 되돌려 놓기 위해 영입되었습니다. 아직 해야 할 일이 많이 남아 있지만, 당신의 리더십 아래 구단이 나아가는 궤적에 대해 이보다 더 만족스러울 수 없습니다. 그리고 채드, 당신은 지난 4월 믿을 수 없을 정도로 어려운 상황에 투입되어 구단이 가장 필요로 할 때 안정감과 리더십을 제공해 주었습니다"라고 치하했습니다.
2006년부터 2014년까지 마이너리그에서 뼈를 깎는 노력을 했으나 선수로서 메이저리그를 밟지 못했던 41세의 트레이시에게는 특히나 감격스러운 하루였습니다. 그 후 그는 2015년부터 코치나 감독으로서 메이저리그에 진출하겠다는 새로운 도전에 나섰습니다.
끈기는 결실을 맺었습니다.
트레이시는 "그렇습니다. 선수와 코치로 보낸 시간을 정확히 합치면 22년이나 됩니다"라며, "정말 긴 시간이었고, 그 모든 순간을 사랑했습니다. 저는 선수로서 이 목표를 이루기 위해 온 힘을 쏟았고, 고등학교 시절부터 확고한 의지를 품었습니다. '나는 야구를 할 것이고 메이저리그 선수가 될 것이다'라고 다짐하며 그것을 실현하기 위해 할 수 있는 모든 노력을 다했습니다. 하지만 여러 장애물들이 가로막아 뜻을 이루지 못했습니다"라고 회상했습니다.
이어 그는 "그리고 나서 저는 야구라는 스포츠를 사랑하고 선수들과 지식을 나누는 것을 좋아하며, 클럽하우스의 일원이 되는 것과 야구 선수들 곁에 있는 것이 좋기 때문에 맨 밑바닥부터 다시 시작해 코치로서 모든 것을 해내겠다고 결심했습니다. 그 여정을 따라 가다 보면, 결국 이 지점에 도달하는 것이 얼마나 멋진 일인지 실감하게 됩니다"라고 덧붙였습니다.
트레이시에게 진정한 의미의 감격스러운 순간은 발표를 축하하는 기자회견이 열리기 전, 트리플A 우스터에서 4년 넘는 기간 동안 자신이 마이너리그에서 직접 지도했던 선수들을 비롯한 선수단과 기쁨을 나눌 때 찾아왔습니다.
트레이시는 "목이 살짝 메였습니다"라며, "그 순간에 서서 그동안의 여정을 되돌아보고, 지난 5년 동안 제 곁을 지켜주었던 선수들의 얼굴들을 둘러보았기 때문입니다. 방 안에 있는 선수들을 둘러보고, 제가 아주 깊은 유대감을 쌓아온 선수들과 함께 그 발표를 나눌 수 있었다는 것은 정말 멋진 순간이었습니다"라고 털어놓았습니다.
또한 그는 "선수들에게 오늘은 양복 재킷을 벗어던지고 유니폼으로 갈아입은 뒤 다시 업무에 복귀하여 선수들 자신과 우리가 10월에 무엇을 해낼 것인지에만 집중하겠다고 말했습니다. 하지만 우리 그룹과 함께한 이번 순간은 정말 특별했습니다"라고 전했습니다.
레드삭스는 6월 25일부터 시작된 32승 5패의 질주를 통해 모든 예상을 뒤엎은 팀이었습니다.
이토록 많은 승리를 거두기 전, 브레슬로의 감독 및 코칭스태프 교체 단행이 당장의 순위에 큰 변화를 주지 못하자 그는 거센 비판과 검증의 대상이 되었습니다. 하지만 구단주 그룹이 비공개로 지속적인 지지를 보내는 동안, 브레슬로는 외부의 소음에 귀를 닫았습니다.
그는 "솔직한 심정을 말씀드리자면, 저와 나머지 프런트오피스는 팀을 어떻게 다시 정상궤도에 올릴 것인지, 어떻게 더 많은 승리를 거둘 것인지, 그리고 선수들이 자신들의 역량을 온전히 발휘할 수 있도록 어떻게 도울 것인지에 너무 몰두해 있었습니다. 덕분에 저 자신에게 무슨 일이 일어날지 걱정할 겨를조차 없었습니다. 야구 운영 부서로서 우리는 오직 '어떻게 이 상황을 뒤집을 것인가?'에만 집착했습니다. 그것이 최우선 과제였고, 우리의 모든 시간을 쏟아부은 대상이었습니다"라고 설명했습니다.
트레이시와 브레슬로가 마주할 다음 과제는 오는 9월 29일 시작되는 아메리칸리그 와일드카드 시리즈를 위해 레드삭스를 철저히 준비시키는 것입니다.
케네디 사장은 "우리가 앞으로 나아가고 가을 야구를 향해 전진함에 따라, 이 구단은 이제 탄탄한 기반 위에 서게 되었습니다"라며, "우리 야구 운영 부서는 이제 연속성과 안정성을 확보했습니다. 우리는 다가올 미래와, 야구계에서 가장 열정적인 우리 팬들에게 그들이 마땅히 받아야 할 선물인 '챔피언십을 위해 싸울 기회'를 안겨줄 수 있는 우리의 능력에 대해 큰 기대와 낙관을 품고 있습니다"라고 강조했습니다.

item.dc:creator: Gabrielle Starr

item.content:encoded:
There were no guarantees on the night of April 25, when Chad Tracy was abruptly pulled from what ultimately became his 499th and final win as Triple-A Worcester manager, and handed the keys to Boston’s big-league kingdom on an interim basis.
Nor the next morning when Tracy, 41, walked into the Camden Yards visitors’ clubhouse in Baltimore to manage his first big-league game, to stunned and upset Red Sox players publicly questioning the future of the organization after the previous night’s firing of longtime manager Alex Cora and six coaches.
The future became clearer on Tuesday morning. Hours before opening the final homestand of 2026, and fresh off clinching a playoff spot for the second consecutive year, the Red Sox officially announced Tracy’s new three-year contract to become their 49th manager, and the exercising of their 2029 and 2030 options on chief baseball officer Craig Breslow.
“When it became time to make the very difficult change in leadership with our major league team, there was kind of really only one name that was considered,” Breslow said as he, Tracy and team president and CEO Sam Kennedy sat in the Fenway Park interview room Tuesday afternoon to discuss the day’s news.
The Red Sox were 10-17, tied for the American League’s worst record, when Tracy arrived. And they got worse before they got better. They lost several stars to injuries in late April and early May, and fell to their worst home record to begin a season since 1932 in early June.
“I mean, it was abysmal,” Kennedy said. “April, May and June were brutal to live through.”
As the losses mounted, so did public perception of Tracy as a stalking horse, and Breslow as a man on borrowed time. But within the organization, Red Sox leadership and players felt a significant shift when Tracy took the reins.
“It became pretty clear early on that Chad was the right person at the right time to lead this group,” Breslow, 46, said. “(We) recognized that this was a fit we wanted to preserve. … I think there was probably some realization a few weeks ago, maybe even further, that there’s a natural conclusion here that we’re working toward.”
The question of Tracy’s future with the organization was present from the start, both internally and externally, but he remained unruffled.
“Yeah, I mean, it didn’t bother me much anyways,” Tracy said. “I worried about the players. I worried about getting us on track, helping get us on track. … That was what my focus was on, and I figured this stuff, if it goes well enough, it’ll come together on its own.”
Tracy took a similar approach to last offseason’s WooSox managerial contract negotiations. Many might try to make the leap to a major league coaching job after managing a Triple-A team to winning seasons in each of their four years at the helm, and spending over two decades playing and working in the minor leagues. But Tracy took the “Que Sera Sera” approach; whatever will be, will be.
“I think those opportunities happen on their own,” Tracy said. “You don’t operate in those jobs thinking about, how do I get to my next one? You just do your job. … I’m here to help people. I’m here to help the players. And if I do that properly, then whether it’s here or somewhere else, those things always take care of themselves.”
Tracy’s unbotheredness by limbo and chaos, and his ability to navigate turbulent waters and help his players do the same were key factors in the removal of the interim tag.
Asked what he learned about Tracy after moving him up to the majors, Breslow said, “The answer to that is maybe what makes Chad most remarkable, which is, he was exactly the same. He was exactly as he was as the manager in Worcester, he was exactly the same after a shutout win as he was a heart-wrenching defeat, and I think that stability, that consistency, is how our players have responded so well.
“So what I’ve learned is he is just an unbelievably intense but even-keeled leader, someone who builds sincere and authentic relationships with everyone that he interacts with and comes across, someone that I think can can be trusted to be honest and questioned when it’s appropriate to do so, and someone who is willing to always put the players in the organization first.”
Members of the Red Sox echoed Breslow’s sentiments.
“I’m happy for him, because he’s handled this amazingly,” veteran shortstop Trevor Story told the Herald. “Odds were kind of stacked against him, and kind of our team in general, too. So happy for him, and he deserves it. He stewarded the ship in an incredible way, so pumped for him that he can kick that interim tag and be here for a while.”
“He’s a real calming influence,” Story continued. “If you talk to him or get to know him at all, he’s very level-headed, really knowledgeable baseball guy, and just being around him is a good feeling. So that goes a long way, I think, to being a manager, and I think yeah, he’s shown that he can handle this whole situation of Boston and everything going on.”
“He’s done an incredible job, just bringing this clubhouse together, and just taking it one day at a time, and I am incredibly happy for him,” catcher and first baseman Mickey Gasper told the Herald. “There’s nobody that’s earned something more that I’ve been around in the game of baseball than Trace, getting this job. He’s done a tremendous job, and I couldn’t think of anybody else better for the role.”
“I’ve learned so much from him,” added Gasper, who played for Tracy on the ‘24 WooSox and split this season between Worcester and Boston. “How to be a baseball man around your teammates, how to bring a fresh slate every day to the ballpark.
“The wins and losses wear on you that day. Playing for Trace the last couple years, even in the minor leagues we’ve had some tough losses together, and he always comes back the next day. Today is a new day. This is the task at hand, and just being able to turn the page after tough spots, tough losses, just adversity in general. And I think just watching him go about his business that’s what I’ve learned the most. He leads by example.”
Those particular attributes also made Tracy an ideal partner for Breslow. The latter must make the difficult decisions, the former has proved adept at ensuring the ripple effects don’t become tsunamis. The Red Sox feel this pairing will provide the stability that has been in scarce supply over the last decade.
“It’s huge,” Kennedy said of locking in this tandem for the next three years. “It’s a sacred relationship, between the head of baseball operations and the manager. Being on the same page, having that trust, that confidence in each other (is) something that I’ve learned going back to my days at the New York Yankees and the San Diego Padres. And here, seeing successful versions of it, and seeing unsuccessful versions of it.
“Lord knows we’ve made mistakes in our time. And just ensuring that you have that relationship right is critical. So yeah, it’s great to have that stability now. And look, we haven’t achieved anything, we know that. But I think we’re set up for success going forward.”
Story was glad to say he felt differently than that morning in Baltimore, when he was one of several longtime Red Sox who wondered “what the true direction of the franchise is.”
“When AC and all the guys got let go, we didn’t know the direction,” Story said. “And now, I feel like we do.”

After an off day on Monday, the Boston Red Sox will return to Fenway Park to begin the next-to-last series of the regular season before the playoffs next week. Boston clinched their spot in the postseason after the Atlanta Braves completed a three-game sweep of the Houston Astros on Sunday afternoon.
The Red Sox are all but locked into the second American League wild-card spot. They are on a collision course with the New York Yankees next week in the Bronx for a best-of-three series. Before then, however, Boston has three games with the Cleveland Guardians. They will then host the Chicago Cubs this weekend, weather permitting.
As for the Guardians series, Wilyer Abreu is back in the lineup for manager Chad Tracy and batting in a familiar spot.
Boston Red Sox Announce Wilyer Abreu Spot in Lineup Against Guardians on Tuesday Night
Tracy will send left-hander Payton Tolle to the mound to open the series and as far as his lineup goes, Abreu us back and batting cleanup. Here is Boston's lineup for the series opener against Cleveland's Parker Messick,
Nick Sogard 1B
Jahmai Jones DH
Wilyer Abreu RF
Caleb Durbin 3B
Isiah Kiner-Falefa SS
Nate Eaton CF
Abreu will be batting fourth, with first baseman Willson Contreras still out of the lineup after getting hit by a pitch last Thursday night against the Texas Rangers. He missed the series against the Tampa Bay Rays. As for Abreu, he did not play in Sunday's series finale, a 5-1 loss.
Boston Red Sox Playing Out the String Ahead of Playoffs
Tuesday, it was announced that Tracy was having the interim tag removed, and Chief Baseball Officer Craig Breslow is having his option in 2029 and 2030 picked up by the club. It's not surprising that it was announced before the playoffs.
Boston is scheduled to send their three projected starters on the mound next week against the Yankees: Tolle, Sonny Gray, and Ranger Suárez against the Guardians. However, Cleveland is in a heated race with the Chicago White Sox for the American League Central Division title. They enter the series with a one-game lead over the White Sox, who are playing the Kansas City Royals this week.
Boston has slumped in September. However, they can use the six games before next week as a tune-up. As for this weekend, the weather is projected to be a mess. Tim Healy of the Boston Globe reported that MLB has no plans to move the series out of Boston. There are going to be very few windows to play baseball this weekend.
The Cubs are in a battle for home-field advantage in the National League wild-card round. Those games will have big meaning for them and the NL. They enter play this week tied with the San Diego Padres for home-field advantage next week. The Philadelphia Phillies are a game behind. There is a lot riding on this weekend.

item.content:encoded:
The Craig Breslow era in Boston has felt like a roller coaster ride. Hired at the start of the 2023-24 offseason, the Boston Red Sox have not had a losing season under Breslow, despite wild swings in the team's form over the three years.
With the Red Sox clinching a playoff berth for the second year in a row, team ownership decided that now was the time to exercise two options on their Chief Baseball Officer's contract, guaranteeing his deal for the 2029 and 2030 seasons. On the surface, a head of baseball operations who got his team to the playoffs in years two and three of their time running the club getting years added to their contract, would make sense, but in Breslow's case it isn't as straightforward.
It was only three months ago when most of Red Sox Nation was calling for Breslow's head. The Red Sox were 32-46 on June 24, dead last in the division, and it already seemed like the season was over. It took a miraculous turnaround to get the team to the playoffs. Not to say that Breslow had nothing to do with that; he had added a lot of players to the roster who were key contributors, but that has a lot more to do with the players and coaches than the front office.
Breslow's tenure has also been marred by controversy, specifically the Rafael Devers drama. It was his handling of the situation, along with former manager Alex Cora, that ultimately led to the fracture of the relationship with the team's then-face of the franchise. While the fanbase was split on whose side they took, player or team, his actions after the fact didn't make it any better.
Red Sox's Craig Breslow had the hottest seat of any GM only three months ago
It was the signing of Alex Bregman that caused the Devers drama in the first place. While Breslow was praised for the signing, Bregman opted out at the end of the year and was then not re-signed. The Red Sox went from two elite third basemen to none in the span of a season. It wasn't a good look for the Red Sox CBO.
Now, Breslow's pivot from all of the drama and mess surrounding Devers and Bregman looks incredibly good in hindsight. The additions of Ranger Suarez, Sonny Gray, Willson Contreras, Caleb Durbin, and others have been extremely impactful to the Red Sox's success this season. While some of those moves were celebrated at the time they happened, others like the Durbin-Kyle Harrison swap (that also netted the Red Sox Andruw Monasterio and Anthony Seigler) were heavily scrutinized.
Breslow also made good moves at the trade deadline, adding Erik Miller and Eli White, who have looked good for the Sox. He also made the splash trade for Adley Rutschman, which hasn't worked as well on the field, but certainly instilled confidence in the team, knowing the front office believed in them.
Red Sox could've softened the impact by extending one of Craig Breslow's options at first
All of this is to say that Breslow's time as CBO hasn't been as smooth sailing as the records would suggest. He has had some high highs but also some low lows. Why did ownership feel the need to exercise both options right now? The first option wasn't needed until the 2029 season, two years out. The second was for 2030, three years out.
Doing the first one now would've been fine — picking up the 2029 option gives Breslow another three comfortable seasons on his contract. That would make him more comfortable making moves for the future and give him the job security to know he will likely be in place to see them play out. Selecting the 2030 option on the same day was unnecessary, though.
There have been too many hiccups in the three years under Breslow to say he has warranted another four seasons. The start of 2026 could easily repeat itself in 2027. Should ownership feel the need to relieve him of his duties early, then this makes it that much harder. Breslow hasn't won a World Series in Boston; in fact, he hasn't even made it out of the Wild Card round. Exercising the option for 2030 feels very premature.
Breslow has not done a bad job in Boston. At the end of the day, it's results that matter, and Breslow's teams have made the playoffs two out of three times. He shouldn't be fearing for his job, but his contract also wasn't ending for another two seasons. It feels early to be handing him the keys so far down the road after the drama of his first two years as CBO.

item.content:encoded:
Garrett Crochet reached an important milestone in his road to recovery on Tuesday, facing live hitters on the mound at Fenway Park for the first time since his ill-fated comeback attempt in late May.
Throwing live batting practice against Ceddanne Rafaela, the Red Sox ace threw 16 pitches, one more than originally planned because he spiked a changeup into the dirt on what was supposed to be his final pitch. The left-hander said he was able to ramp up his intensity to a level he hadn’t reached yet, that his fastball was in the 94-96 mph range, and that following the session he got good feedback from Rafaela.
With that crucial box checked, could Crochet’s next time on the mound come in a game setting? Crochet said it’s too soon to say, but he’s cautiously optimistic about his ability to do so.
“You don’t know until you know I suppose. I would say the way that live just went that I could go get outs,” Crochet said. “It depends, obviously, what role they want me in, like I said it’s not really for me to say, I know myself and I know my body, and the biggest thing is that I felt good out there.”
Crochet has missed the majority of the season due to left shoulder inflammation, which landed him on the injured list in late April after only six starts. What was originally believed to be a short-term injury wound up sidelining Crochet for five months and counting, but after Tuesday’s session there remains a possibility Crochet could factor into the postseason equation for the Red Sox out of the bullpen.
That will be up to chief baseball officer Craig Breslow and manager Chad Tracy, Crochet was sure to emphasize.
“This team has had a great year, I think for me to take a spot on the roster then someone would have to lose one, and I would feel bad doing that because this team has pitched their (butts) off the whole season,” Crochet said. “Ultimately that’s going to be something that’s up to the front office and whenever they gauge that I’m ready then I’ll accept that, and in the meantime I’m just going to keep working my butt off.”
Tracy said he was encouraged by Crochet’s outing, noting that his velocity is climbing and the spin on his pitches looked sharp. The next step will be seeing how his body recovers in the upcoming days and mapping out a plan for the weekend.
“What that looks like now, I don’t know,” Tracy said. “I just know that whatever it is it’s going to be done with Garrett’s best interest in mind.”
Typically the next stage in a throwing progression after throwing live batting practice would be to start a rehab assignment, but given that the minor league season ended this past weekend, that isn’t an option for Crochet. Time also isn’t on the left-hander’s side, so if Crochet is going to pitch in a game before the playoffs, he would have to be activated at some point over the final homestand.
Tracy said those are all factors the club is considering, and while he believes Crochet would be up for the challenge of jumping right into a playoff series, they have to be realistic about where he’s at when it comes time to decide who will be on the playoff roster.
“Knowing the player, if he was healthy and we felt he could he’d probably be like ‘I’m not going to be afraid of that,'” Tracy said. “That being said, we have to consider it and just be very mindful of what are we potentially exposing him to and what can he give us, really? Understanding you don’t want to leave yourself short, so for me it’s been step by step, the next step would be sometime this weekend, let’s see what that entails, and we’ll go from there.”
Rafaela, Contreras getting close
Ceddanne Rafaela (right quad strain) and Willson Contreras (bruised right hand) remain sidelined with their respective injuries, but Tracy said both are getting close to a return.
“(Rafaela) is doing much better, we’re getting close there, and Willson’s also doing much better, he was able to swing pretty aggressively in the cage again today,” Tracy said, adding that Rafaela was scheduled to run and Contreras was set to take batting practice on the field. “(We’ll) let them get through their whole day, see where they’re at and assess, but I think we’re getting pretty close with both of them.”
Staying ready
With the minor league season finished the Red Sox have sent a contingent of players who may potentially factor into the club’s plans the rest of the way to Fort Myers so they can stay ready in the event they’re needed.
Tracy did not have the full list of players available when asked Tuesday, but some of those headed to Fort Myers include pitchers Tanner Houck, Johan Oviedo, Jedixson Paez, Tyler Samaniego and Wyatt Olds, infielders Romy Gonzalez, Franklin Arias and Tsung-Che Cheng, and outfielder Braiden Ward.
Veteran catcher Tomas Nido has also come up from Worcester to serve as an extra catcher on the taxi squad for the Red Sox.
Extra innings
The Red Sox announced Eli White underwent successful Lisfranc repair surgery on his right foot Tuesday. The procedure was performed by Dr. Martin O’Malley at the Hospital for Special Surgery in New York City. … Aroldis Chapman (lat tightness) is feeling much better but is still a day or two away from a return to the mound. … Curtis Mead (fractured left wrist) has resumed swinging a regular bat and is taking overhand batting practice, but while the Red Sox haven’t ruled out a possible return, Tracy acknowledged that time isn’t on his side.

Once again, Garrett Crochet donned a full Red Sox uniform, made the walk from the bullpen to the mound, and pitched at Fenway Park on Tuesday afternoon. This time, he faced a live hitter -- in the form of Ceddanne Rafaela -- as he took another step toward returning to the mound for Boston.
And for the first time in what's been a long recovery period, the 27-year-old said he feels ready to contribute.
"I would say, the way that that live [batting practice] just went, that I could go get outs," Crochet told reporters inside the Red Sox clubhouse.
That being said, Crochet shared that he has some hesitance to joining the roster, though it has nothing to do with his own health.
"This team's had a great year. I think that for me to take a spot on the roster, then someone would have to lose one. And I would feel bad doing that, because this team has pitched their ass off the whole season," Crochet said. "Ultimately, that's something that's gonna be up to the front office. And whenever they gauge that I'm ready, then I'll accept that. In the meantime, I'm just gonna keep working my butt off."
More Red Sox Coverage
Crochet's work on Tuesday involved 16 pitches, and he estimated he was sitting at 94-96 mph on his fastball velocity. The left-hander said how well he recovers on Wednesday will be a significant determinant on his ability to pitch in games. Yet when asked if he'll pitch in a regular-season game this weekend or save his return for the postseason, he is leaving that decision to chief baseball officer Craig Breslow and manager Chad Tracy.
"I think that I'm just gonna do whatever they tell me to do, to be honest," he said. "I think that [live BPs] and games, obviously it's a big step up and the pressure of the moment, I suppose, and the intensity. But I don't think that there's a set amount of [live BPs] that need to be thrown before a game."
Tracy, who officially dropped the interim tag earlier in the day, said that whatever decision is made on Crochet, it will be "done with Garrett's best interests in mind."
"Looking at what is he able to accomplish this week, and what does the playoffs require?" Tracy explained. "And then deciding can he fit that role or not based on what he's done."
Ceddanne Rafaela
Rafaela, who hasn't played since Sept. 2 due to a hamstring injury, partook in the live BP with Crochet as he nears a return to the lineup.
"Much better," Tracy said on Rafaela. "Getting close there."
Rafaela has produced the best offensive season of his career, as he's batted .282 with a .760 OPS in 135 games, while continuing to provide Gold Glove-level defense in center field.
Willson Contreras
Tracy also shared a positive injury update on Willson Contreras, who continues to improve after taking a pitch off his right hand last Thursday.
Tracy said that Contreras is "doing much better" and is "swinging aggressively" as he works his way back to full strength.
Aroldis Chapman
Closer Aroldis Chapman hasn't pitched since Sept. 13 due to some lat tightness, but Tracy had yet another positive injury update.
"He's getting very close," Tracy said. "I think we're a day or two away from him being ready to roll."
Group staying ready in Fort Myers
The Red Sox are keeping a team of reinforcements ready in Fort Myers for the playoff run, in case anybody is needed as an injury replacement along the way. That list of players includes:
- SP Tanner Houck
- SP Johan Oviedo
- SS/2B Franklin Arias
- OF Braiden Ward
- RP Wyatt Olds
- SS/2B Tsung-Che Cheng
- RP Tyler Samaniego
- 1B/2B Romy Gonzalez
- RP Jedixson Paez
Curtis Mead
Perhaps the lone negative injury update from Tracy was on second baseman Curtis Mead, who broke his wrist in his first game with the Red Sox on July 27.
"Haven't ruled it out yet. It's gonna be tough," Tracy said when asked if Mead might be able to return for the first round of the playoffs.
Tracy said that Mead is taking some overhand batting practice, but there may not be enough time for Mead to progress to being game-ready.
"I said we would probably be a little aggressive to see how the hand responds," Tracy said. "Have not ruled it out. It's just we're getting up against it a bit."

It’s hard to say until you know how he feels.”
Tracy will see how the ace feels before making any other decision regarding his injury, giving him time to heal. But the Red Sox have been patiently waiting for Crochet to get back on the mound following his injury back in April.

item.content:encoded:
The Red Sox tied controversial chief baseball officer Craig Breslow's future to the Boston franchise through 2030 on Tuesday, extending his grip on baseball operations after a season that at one point looks like it would have cost him the job.
The move, announced alongside a three-year contract making interim skipper Chad Tracy the club's 49th manager, arrives five months after a coaching purge and a fan revolt threatened to end Breslow's tenure early.
Born in New Haven and raised in nearby Trumbull, Connecticut, Breslow grew up attending Congregation B'nai Israel in Bridgeport, where he had his bar mitzvah in 1993. His older sister's childhood cancer diagnosis, when Breslow was 12, pointed him toward medicine long before baseball made that detour permanent.
Red Sox Turbulence Under Breslow
Breslow retired as a player following a stint with the Cleveland franchise, then called the Indians, in 2017. He stated a new baseball career in the front office in 2019, when Theo Epstein brought him to the Chicago Cubs as director of strategic initiatives. He rose to assistant general manager and senior vice president of pitching before the Red Sox hired him as chief baseball officer in October 2023, replacing Chaim Bloom.
His tenure produced long-term extensions for core players such as Brayan Bello, Garrett Crochet and Roman Anthony — and no shortage of turbulence. The 2025 trade of Rafael Devers to the San Francisco Giants reportedly fractured his standing in the clubhouse, and ESPN's Jeff Passan reported Breslow's circle of trust had narrowed, with one loyalist warning that "turncoats" were plotting against him internally.
Criticism intensified in April 2026, when Breslow fired manager Alex Cora and six coaches following a 10-17 start. A plane towed a banner over Fenway Park demanding his firing, and Boston Globe columnist Dan Shaughnessy branded his player evaluations "horrendous."
Team president Sam Kennedy insisted that June that dismissing Breslow was "not even on the table", even as national voices called it nearly impossible to picture Breslow surviving the year.
The the turnaround happened. From a 32-46 low point, the club reeled off a 15-game win streak from July 3 to July 22 went 38-16 in July and August clinching their second straight postseason berth on Sunday.
"When you reach a certain level of conviction, you have to act," Breslow said of the gambles that defined his season, according to The Boston Globe's Alex Speier.
Kennedy cited that same conviction Tuesday in explaining the new deal.
"Results matter greatly in this business, but so do judgment, character, and the ability to bring out the best in others," Kennedy said in a statement posted by the team — a verdict on Breslow's most scrutinized season yet.
Breslow's Path to Boston Red Sox Top Job
He captained Trumbull High School's baseball and soccer teams before enrolling at Yale, where he led the Ivy League with a 2.56 ERA as a senior and graduated in 2002 with a molecular biophysics and biochemistry degree. He deferred admission to NYU's medical school to chase a professional pitching carer, a gamble that later earned him The Wall Street Journal's "Smartest Man in Baseball" label and a No. 1 spot on The Sporting News' smartest athletes list.
The Milwaukee Brewers drafted him in the 26th round in 2002, and he debuted with the San Diego Padres in 2005. Breslow pitched 12 big league seasons for seven organizations, posting a 3.45 ERA over 576 appearances, with his sharpest stretch coming during with the Red Sox during Boston's 2013 title run, when he posted a 1.81 ERA and didn't allow an earned run in nine of 10 postseason outings. That championship made Breslow one of only four former Red Sox players to later run the club's baseball department.

item.content:encoded:
After a rollercoaster of a season which included a brutal start, sudden managerial firings, historic win streaks and a playoff clinch, the Boston Red Sox have extended the man who brought it all together. Boston has removed Chad Tracy's "interim" tag and made him their manager, first reported by Christopher Smith of MassLive.
Tracy and the Red Sox have agreed to a three-year contract with a club option in 2030, per Smith. His salary has not yet been reported.
Tracy was Boston's Triple-A manager on April 25, the day Alex Cora and six other members of his coaching staff were fired. The Red Sox then flew him out to Baltimore to take over in a whirlwind and a leap of faith, and it worked. He'll be the 49th manager in Red Sox franchise history (subscription required).
The Red Sox had a 10-17 record on the day of Tracy's promotion and he managed the club to two games below .500 by July 12, the start of the All-Star break. Boston's historic 15-game winning streak had already begun by then — it rallied to sweep the New York Yankees in four games two weeks before, lost a series to the Washington Nationals, and it was all winning from there.
Red Sox name Chad Tracy manager through 2029, exercised club options to keep Craig Breslow CBO through 2030
Tracy had long been revered as the manager of the WooSox and it didn't take long for Red Sox fans to become equally endeared to him. His direct, but friendly communication style offered a stark contrast to other leaders in the organization. He had preexisting relationships with many of the organization's young players from their time in Triple-A and from rehab assignments, and it showed. After the Red Sox's historic July and August spell, Tracy's promotion seemed almost inevitable, and rightfully so.
Within the Tracy contract announcement, the Red Sox also included another contract update. The Red Sox have exercised the 2029-30 club options on Craig Breslow's contract, essentially extending him for another two years.
This is quite a sign of trust from Boston. Breslow's tenure started with some massive moves like the Garrett Crochet trade, and the Red Sox made the playoffs for the first time in three seasons with him at the helm. But his communication style has been criticized, it's led to massive trades of players who were supposed to be fixtiures of the organization for years to come, and front office leaks have marred his public image.
But Breslow has loosened up a bit since the beginning of the season. He's been pictured around the players more often and has been cracking jokes on his radio appearances.
There's also no denying that he had a great 2025-26 offseason. Sonny Gray, Willson Contreras, Ranger Suarez and Caleb Durbin, all acquired by Breslow over the offseason, are all major parts of the Red Sox's success.
Cora had been Boston's manager for eight seasons and many Red Sox fans couldn't stand Breslow at the beginning of June. Things can change quickly in baseball.

El gran repunte de los Red Sox durante la segunda mitad de la temporada ya tiene recompensa. Boston retiró este martes el interinato de Chad Tracy y lo nombró oficialmente como el mánager número 49 en la historia de la franquicia.
Tracy, de 41 años, firmó un contrato por tres temporadas que lo mantendrá en el cargo hasta 2029, además de incluir una opción del club para 2030.
El anuncio llegó apenas dos días después de que Boston asegurara un lugar de comodín para los playoffs.
Tracy asumió el puesto en abril, luego de que los Red Sox despidieran a Alex Cora tras un inicio de 10-17.
Desde entonces, el equipo cambió por completo el rumbo y consiguió una marca de 74-55 bajo las órdenes de Tracy.
Durante ese periodo, Boston hiló 15 victorias consecutivas, una racha que igualó el récord de la franquicia establecido en 1946.
Además, entre el 3 de julio y el 7 de agosto, los Red Sox tuvieron marca de 27-3, un porcentaje de .900 que representó el mejor tramo de 30 juegos en la historia del equipo.
El cambio fue todavía más notable si se toma en cuenta que el 24 de junio Boston tenía récord de 32-46 y estaba a 15 juegos y medio del liderato del Este de la Liga Americana.
También ratifican a Craig Breslow
La organización también confirmó la continuidad de Craig Breslow, director de operaciones de béisbol, al ejercer sus opciones para las temporadas 2029 y 2030.
Breslow, de 46 años, llegó al puesto en octubre de 2023. Antes fue jugador de los Red Sox y formó parte del equipo campeón de la Serie Mundial de 2013.
Es apenas el cuarto exjugador de Boston que encabeza las operaciones de béisbol de la franquicia.
Durante sus tres temporadas al frente, los Red Sox acumularon una marca de 254-226, con porcentaje de .529, la tercera mejor de la Liga Americana.
Antes de llegar a las Grandes Ligas, Tracy dirigió durante cuatro temporadas completas a los Worcester WooSox, la sucursal Triple-A de los Red Sox, desde 2022.
En cada una de esas campañas consiguió un récord ganador.
Su experiencia como mánager también incluye siete años dentro del sistema de ligas menores de los Angelinos de Los Ángeles.
Como jugador, Tracy fue seleccionado en la tercera ronda del draft de 2006 por los Rangers de Texas, procedente de la Universidad de Pepperdine.
Jugó ocho temporadas profesionales, entre 2006 y 2013, dentro de las organizaciones de los Rangers, los Rockies de Colorado y los Reales de Kansas City.
El presidente y director ejecutivo de los Red Sox, Sam Kennedy, destacó el trabajo realizado por Breslow y Tracy durante el proceso de reconstrucción del equipo.
Sobre Breslow, señaló que durante los últimos tres años aportó claridad, disciplina y convicción para construir la operación de béisbol.
Respecto a Tracy, Kennedy destacó que asumió una situación complicada con poco tiempo de preparación y rápidamente ganó la confianza dentro del equipo.

La directiva del equipo bostoniano retiró el interinato de Chad Tracy firmándolo hasta 2029 tras amarrar su boleto de comodín a los playoffs.
Los Boston Red Sox disputarán la Postemporada de las Grandes Ligas tras firmar un regreso espectacular en la segunda mitad de la campaña regular, y la directiva no tardó en recompensar a los dos grandes arquitectos del resurgimiento en las Mayores.
Este martes, la franquicia anunció de manera oficial la remoción del interinato del timonel Chad Tracy para nombrarlo el mánager número 49 en la historia de la organización, otorgándole un contrato por tres temporadas que lo vincula hasta el final de la campaña 2029 con una opción del club para 2030.
A la par, el equipo anunció la extensión del contrato del presidente de operaciones de beisbol, Craig Breslow, al ejercer sus opciones institucionales para 2029 y 2030.
¿Cómo logró Chad Tracy la ratificación como mánager de Red Sox?
La consolidación de Tracy, de 41 años de edad, llega apenas dos días después de que Boston asegurara uno de los boletos de comodín a la fiesta grande de la Liga Americana.
El estratega tomó las riendas del vestidor en el mes de abril de manera intempestiva tras el cese de Alex Cora, quien dejó el cargo luego de un convulso arranque de temporada con marca de 10-17.
Desde su nombramiento, Tracy guió a los Patirrojos a un récord de 74-55, incluyendo una racha de 15 victorias consecutivas que igualó la marca histórica de la franquicia impuesta en 1946.

El respaldo de la directiva y la trayectoria de Craig Breslow
A través de un comunicado institucional, el presidente y CEO de los Red Sox, Sam Kennedy, resaltó la labor realizada por el cuerpo técnico y la plana mayor para revertir el panorama deportivo.
"En los últimos tres años, hemos visto a Craig aportar claridad, disciplina y convicción al trabajo de construir nuestras operaciones de beisbol. Se le pidió a Chad asumir una situación difícil con muy poco margen de aviso, pero la confianza que inspiró de inmediato a nivel de Grandes Ligas se la ganó tras años de trabajo en nuestra organización. Lo que este equipo ha logrado durante los últimos meses ha sido histórico", señaló el directivo.
Breslow, de 46 años y campeón de la Serie Mundial de 2013 con Boston como lanzador, asumió el cargo ejecutivo en octubre de 2023.
Durante sus tres campañas al frente del proyecto deportivo, los Red Sox registran una marca global de 254-226 (.529), ostentando el tercer mejor récord de toda la Liga Americana.

Los Boston Red Sox tomaron una decisión importante de cara a su futuro y anunciaron que Chad Tracy deja de ser manager interino para convertirse oficialmente en el entrenador del equipo. El acuerdo tendrá vigencia hasta la temporada 2029.
La organización también ejerció las opciones contractuales de Craig Breslow para las campañas 2029 y 2030, por lo que ambos continuarán al frente del proyecto de Boston durante los próximos años.
Chad Tracy recibe la confianza de Boston
Tracy asumió el puesto el pasado 26 de abril, cuando reemplazó a Alex Cora después de que los Red Sox comenzaran la campaña con marca de 10-17. Desde entonces, el equipo protagonizó una importante recuperación.
Bajo su dirección, Boston consiguió asegurar un lugar en los playoffs de la Liga Americana y llegó a registrar una impresionante marca de 27-3 entre el 3 de julio y el 7 de agosto, el mejor periodo de 30 partidos en la historia de la franquicia.
El trabajo de Tracy permitió que los Red Sox pasaran de un complicado inicio de temporada a conseguir su boleto a la postemporada. El equipo anunció que será el manager número 49 en la historia de la organización.
Craig Breslow también continuará en Boston
La continuidad no será exclusiva de Tracy, pues los Red Sox también decidieron mantener a Craig Breslow como Chief Baseball Officer. La organización ejerció sus opciones contractuales correspondientes a 2029 y 2030.
Breslow asumió ese cargo en octubre de 2023 y durante su gestión Boston ha construido un proyecto que ahora tendrá continuidad con Tracy en el dugout. Los términos económicos de ambos acuerdos no fueron revelados.
Con estas decisiones, los Red Sox aseguran la continuidad de dos de las figuras que han encabezado la transformación del equipo durante 2026. Tracy y Breslow ahora tendrán la responsabilidad de preparar a Boston para las próximas temporadas.

There will not be institutional turnover this upcoming offseason for the Boston Red Sox.
In April, the Red Sox fired former manager Alex Cora, along with a handful of coaches. At the time, Boston's season was sputtering out of control and the Red Sox turned the reins over to Chad Tracy as the club's interim manager and the rest is history. The first few months weren't great and it seemed like everyone's seat was getting hotter and hotter. But Boston stayed the course and turned its season around. The Red Sox met the moment and already have put themselves in the record books as the team with the worst 75-game start (31-44) by a team to make the playoffs in MLB history.
Now, the interim tag is coming off Tracy and the Red Sox don't need to think about it or have the decision hang over the club throughout the rest of the season. Boston announced on Tuesday that it has signed Tracy to a three-year deal with a 2030 club option. That's not all, though. Boston also announced that chief baseball officer Craig Breslow has had his 2029 and 2030 club options exercised as well.
"The Red Sox today announced that they have exercised the club’s 2029 and 2030 contract options on Chief Baseball Officer Craig Breslow and named Chad Tracy the team’s 49th manager in club history, agreeing to a three-year contract that will run through the 2029 season with a club option in 2030," the Red Sox announced.
The Red Sox Got It Right
Boston got it right.
With Tracy leading the charge, the Red Sox have gone 74-55. Boston tied its franchise record for the longest winning streak in team history at 15 back in July. That's not all, though. Boston also went on the best 35-game stretch in franchise history throughout the summer when it went 30-5, which was the 26th time in the World Series Era (1903-present) that a team was able to reach this feat in general.
Tracy came into the picture and picked up a team that was dealing with injuries all over the place and led the way with a steady hand. The team loves him. The fans love him. And now, he's not going anywhere. The timing couldn't be better as well with the postseason a week away from kicking off. The decision has been made and it doesn't have to linger or hang over the team any longer. The full focus can be on the task at hand: winning games and making a run.
The same can be said about Breslow, and this is also the right call. As Boston struggled early in the summer, his job security certainly was talked about. Boston has shown in recent memory that it isn't afraid to move on from a decision-maker at the top of the baseball operations department. The Red Sox were struggling and it seemed like Breslow would fall victim to that in the offseason.
Then, the Red Sox transformed their season and now is in a much different place. Boston is getting healthier and went out and added pieces, including Adley Rutschman. We're starting to see how good this roster that Breslow built can be. Now, he has more job security. Again, this is the right call. It took a while for the baseball world to truly see it, but Breslow built a winner that has a real shot at winning the World Series this season.

The Boston Red Sox today announced that they have exercised the club’s 2029 and 2030 contract options on Chief Baseball Officer Craig Breslow and named Chad Tracy the team’s 49th manager in club history, agreeing to a three-year contract that will run through the 2029 season with a club option in 2030.
“Craig and Chad are two exceptionally talented leaders who have earned these opportunities in very different ways,” said Red Sox President & CEO Sam Kennedy. “Over the last three years, we have watched Craig bring clarity, discipline, and conviction to the work of building our baseball operation. Chad was asked to step into a difficult situation with little notice, but the trust he immediately commanded at the major league level was earned through years of work across our organization. What this team has accomplished over the past several months has been historic. Results matter greatly in this business, but so do judgment, character, and the ability to bring out the best in others. Craig and Chad have demonstrated all of those qualities, and they have earned our confidence in leading us forward.”
Breslow, 46, was hired as Chief Baseball Officer on October 25, 2023. A 2013 World Series champion with Boston, Breslow is only the fourth former Red Sox player to lead the club’s baseball operations efforts, the first since Haywood Sullivan served as General Manager from 1978-83. During his three seasons in his current role, the Red Sox have gone 254-226 (.529), the third-best record in the American League and ninth best in the Majors.
Prior to his 2023 hiring, Breslow spent the previous five seasons in the Chicago Cubs organization, most recently as Assistant General Manager/Senior Vice President, Pitching in 2023. His front office career began in 2019 with the Cubs as Director of Strategic Initiatives, evaluating and implementing data-based processes throughout all facets of Baseball Operations while also supporting the pitching infrastructure in the farm system. In 2020 he was named Director of Pitching/Special Assistant to the President and General Manager, then spent the 2021-22 seasons as Assistant General Manager/Vice President, Pitching.
Tracy, 41, made his Major League debut as Interim Manager on April 26. After entering that day tied for the American League’s second-worst record (10-17, .370), the Red Sox’ 74-55 (.574) record since is the second best in the AL and fifth best in the Majors.
Under Tracy, Boston posted the best 30-game span in franchise history, going 27-3 (.900) from July 3 through August 7. That stretch included a club-record-tying 15-game winning streak from July 3 through July 22-G1, a streak matched only by the 1946 Red Sox. Boston’s 21-4 (.840) record during July marked the club’s best winning percentage ever in a calendar month (minimum 20 games) and the third-best record of any Major League club during July.
A native of Illinois, Tracy earned his 499th career minor league managerial win on April 25, one day before being named Boston’s interim manager. He had served as Triple-A Worcester’s manager since 2022, leading the WooSox to a winning record in each of his four full seasons as manager (2022-25). Tracy spent the previous seven seasons (2015-21) in the Los Angeles Angels system, including three as a minor league manager with Low-A Burlington (2015) and High-A Inland Empire (2016-17). He served as the Angels’ minor league field coordinator from 2018-21.
Selected by the Texas Rangers in the third round of the 2006 First-Year Player Draft out of Pepperdine University, Tracy played eight professional seasons (2006-13) in the Rangers, Colorado Rockies, and Kansas City Royals organizations. While at Pepperdine (2004-06), he earned West Coast Conference Player of the Year and First-Team All-Conference honors in 2005.

Even with the Red Sox having secured their second straight postseason berth, the magnitude of Craig Breslow’s gamble five months ago remains startling.
There have been times when teams reacted to slow starts with a managerial or coaching staff change. But longtime members of the industry could not recall anything like the shakeup enacted by Breslow in April, when he fired manager Alex Cora and replaced six other members of the coaching staff.
It was a move that departed from convention both for when it happened (barely a month into the season) and the extent of the change. It also pointed to an emerging theme of Breslow’s time as chief baseball officer: The willingness of the Sox to take significant in-season risks.
The firing of Cora and the staff members (with replacements plucked from the minors with little big league clubhouse experience), the mid-June trade of Rafael Devers in 2025, and the acquisition of catcher Adley Rutschman in exchange for a package of young talent (four of the Sox’ top 10 prospects, as well as catcher Carlos Narváez) that exceeded any in-season move by the Sox this century all pointed to an organization making massive bets on in-season changes.
“I always try to be guided by what I believe to be right and best for the organization,” Breslow said of his in-season risk tolerance. “Oftentimes, most people in these jobs would say their initial read or inclination of a situation was largely a correct one, but friction and inertia and emotion prevented you from acting on that. Then, you look back and say I wish I would have done whatever it was you were thinking at the time more often than you say that was probably not the right decision, and I wish I hadn’t.
“When you evaluate decisions through that lens, I think I default to, when you reach a certain level of conviction, you have to act.”
That sounds straightforward, but given baseball’s 162-game schedule, there’s often a willingness by heads of baseball operations to let situations play out over larger samples rather than intervene quickly. On both a personal and organizational level, a major in-season shakeup is uncomfortable.
“I certainly don’t sleep well [after a major change] for a few reasons, mostly because these are people that you have relationships with, and it’s not the outcome that you were looking for,” said Breslow. “These decisions are incredibly difficult. We’re talking about people’s lives, their families, children … there are a lot of implications to making these changes. So, it is wildly uncomfortable.”
Still, in a view perhaps informed by his playing career, Breslow has learned to remain open to uncomfortable in-season change — not for its own sake, but instead as a course correction when he sees a path to improving the club.
“I try to balance my [playing] experiences with what more information is telling me,” Breslow said. “I don’t think if I were only looking through things as I had experienced them that that would necessarily position us to make better decisions. But I think ignoring them would be ignoring valuable insights that I’ve learned.
“I was a lefthanded reliever that bounced around, who didn’t find success early on, pretty consistently evaluated the information that my performance was telling me, and tried to make adjustments as quickly as possible. I didn’t have the luxury of infinite runway in front of me to figure things out over time. If that’s an attitude or approach that I take to this job, then I think that’s OK.”
Breslow’s playing career may also inform his approach to in-season risks in another way: The way he values the chance to contend for a title.
It certainly would have been understandable if the Sox had decided by mid-June — around their 32-46 nadir — that they were open for business in a sell-off. Indeed, the Sox were at least starting to prepare for such an eventuality, with some of their pro scouts assigned to organizations who might be interested in short-term veterans, particularly Sonny Gray (who will be a free agent after 2026).
That said, Breslow had experience as a player of a long-shot team emerging as a champion. And so, even though there were few precedents for a team such as the Sox to overcome their long odds, based on his belief in the talent of the group, Breslow wanted to give the team as much time as possible to compete, respecting what he referred to as “the sanctity of a season.”
“Maybe that is born out of my playing career and the fact that the Red Sox won the World Series in 2013 as an improbable group going into the season,” he said. “Fundamentally, my confidence and belief in the players that we had on our roster [in 2026] had not changed. Players didn’t become meaningfully less talented. My belief in the roster was consistent.”
“But it’s interesting. Everybody who sits in my seat is going to talk about sustainability and the ability to compete for championships every single year. I think it’s very important to balance that with acknowledging the importance of every individual season. Otherwise, you talk about windows and about how maybe this isn’t the year, but that’s OK because next year we’ll still have the core of a really good team.
“I have learned that sometimes really good teams don’t have the seasons that they want. Sometimes teams that you don’t have maybe the highest expectations far outperform them for a season’s length. So you don’t want to dismiss what is immediately in front of you in exchange for this idea of lumping seasons together and just kind of thinking about being in the midst of a window.”
And so, the Sox ended up doing the opposite of what everyone forecast. A team for whom a veteran sell-off seemed almost inevitable instead ended up — thanks to one of the great runs in franchise history from late June to mid-August — taking big swings for deadline upgrades with moves to add infielder Curtis Mead and Rutschman.
In different ways, both moves stunned the industry given what the Sox gave up (Connelly Early for Mead; prospects Anthony Eyanson, Kyson Witherspoon, Enddy Azocar, and Harold Rivas, as well as Narváez for Rutschman). But from afar, Rangers president of baseball operations Chris Young — like Breslow, a former player — could appreciate what his colleague did.
“In general, careers are short, and I want every player that puts on our uniform to have a chance to compete for a World Series. That should be our goal as an organization,” said Young. “When you have a team that’s in a win cycle, you need to be bold at times to go for it.
“It doesn’t mean necessarily you’re going to sustain success, but the goal is not to just make the playoffs. The goal is to win championships. And for me, especially in 2023 when we made very bold moves, it led to [a championship]. It easily could not have, but I know that if we didn’t make those moves, we wouldn’t have won. [And] there’s no doubt the player in me is influenced by the opportunity to win.”
Breslow’s deadline deals were motivated by a similar hunger. Now that the Red Sox have qualified for the playoffs, the ultimate impact of the bets made by Breslow in what he repeatedly described as a “difficult” season will gain greater definition in the postseason tournament.
But regardless of what happens, the path to get to the playoffs represented a fascinating shift in how the Red Sox conducted business, in a fashion that defied expectations at numerous turns on and off the field.

The Boston Red Sox's Wild Card clinching ceremony included the usual champagne showers and dripping-wet interviews. Everyone had their moments between the clubhouse party and the team photo, but the expected star of the celebration did not disappont.
Payton Tolle gave Red Sox fans everything they wanted and more out of their playoff-making party. The towering lefty is usually the most hilarious member of the Red Sox, but his antics were turned up to 11 in the presence of more beer than anyone can drink.
Tolle smashed some beers Stone Cold style, danced like no one was watching and gave an under-the-influence interview fans won't soon forget. The best part is that he would probably do many of the same things sober as a judge.
Tolle has grown in to a Red Sox fan favorite in record time. His off-the-field shenanigans match up to the skill he brings on the mound. After his first season-plus with Boston, it should be doing everything in its power to keep Tolle on the team for as long as possible.
Payton Tolle's Wild Card celebration showed just how badly the Red Sox need to extend him
The Red Sox have adopted an early contract extension strategy with many of its young players, including Ceddanne Rafaela, Brayan Bello and Roman Anthony, among others. Alex Speier of The Boston Globe reported on August 18 that Boston hadn't approached Tolle about an extension at the time (subscription required). The Sox have signed so many young players that they could be taking a break, but they should re-start negotiations again for Tolle.
Not only is the 23-year-old an electric personality, he's a force on the mound. The American League's 2026 rookie class is packed to the brim with talent including Kevin McGonigle (the certain winner), Parker Messick and Munetaka Murakami, but Tolle has performed well enough to deserve a mention near the top of this year's list.
Tolle has posted a 3.02 ERA, 1.07 WHIP, 166 strikeouts and 38 walks over 143 innings. The rookie has deepened and sharpened his arsenal this season, his extension (a metric Craig Breslow loves) is elite at a staggering seven-foot-four, his 36.5 percent chase rate sits in the 96th percentile and his 28.9 strikeout percentage ranks near the top of the league. Tolle is an imposing presence on the mound with the prime of his career still years away and the Red Sox should hold onto him for as long as possible.
Tolle will most likely get a start during Boston's Wild Card series, possibly in Game 1. The Red Sox clearly trust him in big moments, he's got personality to share and he's already active in the community — he is the ideal candidate for an early contract extension.

ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — After all the champagne bottles had been emptied and all the beer had been consumed or sprayed, a lone figure emerged from the joyous Red Sox clubhouse late Sunday afternoon.
Red Sox chief baseball officer Craig Breslow was barefoot, his clothes somewhat damp from the proceedings inside, and his sense of satisfaction evident.
Back in late April, Breslow had made the boldest of moves when he fired popular manager Alex Cora and most of his coaching staff, and replaced him with a manager with no major league experience — playing, coaching or managing — and a makeshift coaching staff.
At the time, Breslow said the changes were necessary to save an underperforming team in a season that was quickly slipping away. But in his mind, these Red Sox could still be salvaged. More than once, he mentioned that the Red Sox, then owners of a 10-17 record, still had 135 games left to play.
To many, it seemed like a thin rationalization. As it turned out, Breslow was correct and Sunday, as the Red Sox assured themselves of a playoff spot, he appeared almost prophetic.
“This has been a turbulent season,” said Breslow. “But ultimately, we talked about putting together a team that was capable of getting to the postseason and having a deep postseason run. This (getting into the playoffs) is certainly an accomplishment, but it’s not the primary objective here, so we still have a bunch of important games ahead of us.”
Asked if he had truly believed that the Red Sox were capable of this kind of turnaround, he didn’t hesitate to respond in the affirmative.
“I believed in the players that we had and I believed it was really important to act definitively and decisively when we did, so that we could create an environment around the players that was supportive, that would allow them to thrive, and they responded.
“And while there may have been some people who questioned what this group was capable of, I think they answered resoundingly.”
On Sunday, Breslow singled out interim manager Chad Tracy for extra praise.
“I talked about Trace back in April and just the consistency and stabilizing presence that he can be,” said Breslow. “He’s got an incredibly unique ability to connect with players — young players, veteran players — and I think they really respect the authenticity and the honesty that he approaches them with daily.”
As Breslow spoke, it was hard not to hear some indirect criticism of Cora and the coaches with whom he was most closely associated.
Recounting the 32-5 run that lifted the Red Sox from the division basement, Breslow referenced how the Sox had, after the firings, changed “the way that we practiced, the way that we trained, the way that we delivered information to our players, the way we supported our players. When you put all those things together, they compound and ultimately the performance on the field, by way of wins and losses, was the last thing to catch up.”
Breslow said he noticed a sense of pride displayed by the players as they celebrated qualifying for the postseason for the second straight season and detected some satisfaction in proving their naysayers wrong.
“I think we’ve shown what we’re capable of,” he said.
As a player, Breslow was part of a long playoff run that resulted in a World Series championship in 2013. Now, as an executive, he’s experiencing it from a different perspective.
“The obvious difference is,” he said, “I didn’t have a direct impact on outcomes of games in this role, whereas I did as a player. But I think there’s a different set of gratification when you’re part of this massive effort to identify players and bring them in and help support the coaching staff. It’s very different and in some ways it’s maybe a couple of layers removed. But it’s certainly as satisfying.”
