It’s not remotely the right time to start talking about offseason movement, but there is movement afoot. Two of Craig Breslow’s assistant GMs, Mike Groopman and Taylor Smith, have already conducted preliminary interviews for the big chair in Sacramento after the A’s fired Dave Forst back in August. (Sean McAdam, MassLive)
Here in Boston, though, we’re unlikely to see a search for a new boss in a while. Craig Breslow earned himself quite a bit of rope this season, thanks to a decisive move that paid off big time in firing Alex Cora. “I believed in the players that we had, and I felt it was really important that we acted definitively and decisively when we did, so that we could create an environment around the players that was supportive, that would allow them to thrive, and they responded,” he said. “And, while there may have been some people that questioned what this group was capable of, I think they answered.” (Peter Abraham, Boston Globe)
And here’ s a look at some of the key moments of the season that got this team where it is today. Remember the ninth inning comeback against the Mets that came after that long-delayed flight? How about Caleb Durbin’s home run off Cam Schlittler? (Tim Healey, Boston Globe)
But, strangely enough, when it came time to clinch the playoffs, it wasn’t a Red Sox player who did the dirty work, though it was a Red Sox legacy player. “And the man with the game-winning three-run homer that would, in the end, send both the Braves and the Red Sox to the postseason? Well, baseball is quite sentimental, and it also has a sense of humor, so, obviously, it was Mike Yastrzemski.“ (Shanthi Sepe-Chepuru, MLB.com)
But the fact that the Sox clinched on a loss didn’t dampen the celebration. “There was a lot of beer!” said Payton Tolle. “It was a slobberknocker.” (Rob Bradford, WEEI)
But before the slobberknocker could get slobbin’, Chad Tracy addressed his team to sum up the season that was. “I want to express gratitude for everyone in the room,” he said. “I’m so grateful for you guys, for our staff, for everybody. You stared impossible in the face. The position we were in, you beat it back and said, ‘The hell with that, we’re going to the playoffs.’ And you did.” (Jen McCaffrey, The Athletic)
So the Sox are in the dance. But for how long? That’s anyone’s guess, but Red Sox fans are apparently more optimistic than the fans of any other American league team. (Stephen J. Nesbitt, The Athletic)

The Boston Red Sox have secured a spot in baseball's postseason, making history by becoming the first team to clinch a playoff berth after being 14 games below .500. As of Sunday (September 20), the Red Sox have achieved an 84-72 record under interim manager Chad Tracy, following a remarkable second-half surge. Their playoff spot was confirmed with the Houston Astros' loss to the Atlanta Braves.
Despite a 5-1 loss to the Tampa Bay Rays, the Red Sox celebrated their postseason berth with a clubhouse party. The team, led by spiritual leader Willson Contreras, has shown resilience throughout the season. Tracy, who took over from Alex Cora on April 26, has been credited with stabilizing the team and fostering a supportive environment.
The Red Sox's journey to the playoffs included a significant turnaround starting with a four-game sweep of the New York Yankees in late June. They went on to achieve a 15-game winning streak, tying a franchise record set in 1946. This impressive run has positioned them as the No. 5 seed, likely facing the Yankees in the AL Wild Card round.
The team overcame early-season challenges, including the dismissal of Cora and several coaches. Chief Baseball Officer Craig Breslow emphasized the importance of decisive action in creating a thriving environment for the players. Looking ahead, the Red Sox aim to continue their momentum into the postseason, with the first game of the Wild Card Series expected to take place at Yankee Stadium on September 29.

ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — Craig Breslow stood in a puddle of beer in his stocking feet on Sunday, watching the team he assembled celebrate having clinched its spot in the postseason.
That’s when he realized he still had his phone in his pocket. The Red Sox chief baseball officer carefully picked his way down the hallway to put it out of harm’s way before he got even more soaked.
“Smart move,” Breslow was told.
“It might be too late,” he said, laughing.
You can always get a new phone. But how often can you enjoy the satisfaction of proving that an entire city, if not an entire industry, was wrong?
Breslow made what still remains the most stunning move of this baseball season when he fired Alex Cora and six of his coaches on April 25 after only 27 games.
He was convinced the team had potential it would not realize under Cora and needed a change.
“I believed in the players that we had, and I felt it was really important that we acted definitively and decisively when we did, so that we could create an environment around the players that was supportive, that would allow them to thrive, and they responded,” he said.
“And, while there may have been some people that questioned what this group was capable of, I think they answered.”
Some people? How about most of us?
It was not a straight line to success. The Sox were 13-16 in the first 29 games under interim manager Chad Tracy, and I wrote in late May that it was time to start rebuilding by getting a jump on the trade deadline.
With Roman Anthony and Garrett Crochet on the injured list, it seemed obvious the Sox weren’t going to contend. There were loud “sell the team” chants at Fenway Park.
Tracy’s record was 22-29 three weeks later, and even the players had started to question what was going on at Fenway Park.
“We’re not good. We’re just not a good team right now. That’s just a fact,” righthander Sonny Gray said after a 3-2 loss against the Blue Jays on June 18.
I wrote the next day that it felt inevitable the Sox would be sellers and could well finish the season with 95 losses. Some executives from other teams believed Breslow could only save his job by turning veterans into prospects.
You know what happened next. The Sox went on a season-saving 32-6 run and are now a threat to make a deep run into October. They are the first team in history to lose 44 of their first 75 games and make the playoffs.
“You stared impossible in the face with the position we were in,” Tracy told his players on Sunday.
Breslow did not see any particular series or moment as a turning point.
“I think the turnaround was the result of incremental change, incremental improvement, changes to the way that we practice, the ways that we trained, the way that we delivered information to our players, the way that we supported our players,” he said.
“So I think when you put all those things together, they compound, and then ultimately the performance on the field by way of wins and losses was the last thing to catch up.”
Breslow spent 12 seasons pitching in the majors and grew a beard with the rest of the wild bunch Red Sox of 2013. He appeared in 10 of the 16 playoff games that season and got three huge outs in the eighth inning of Game 6 in the ALCS.
His job now is giving others that opportunity. But in the end, you’re standing in the same puddle of beer with a big smile.
“The obvious difference is I didn’t have a direct impact on the outcomes of games in this role, whereas I did as a player,” Breslow said. “But I think there’s a different sense of gratification when you’re kind of part of this massive effort to identify players and bring them in and help support the coaching staff.
“It’s very different, and in some ways it’s maybe a couple of layers removed. But it’s certainly as satisfying.”
Breslow has earned that satisfaction. The job’s not over, but he had it right about this team.

At one point this season, Boston Red Sox Chief Baseball Officer Craig Breslow was on the hot seat. More than just being on the hot seat, he was presumed to be getting fired by just about everyone as the Red Sox scuffled out of the gate this season.
That’s all a bit different now. The Red Sox have clinched a spot in the playoffs after a shocking mid-season turnaround. With that, Breslow appears to be safe in his job.
That doesn’t mean that Breslow doesn’t still have his critics. That’s part of the job, after all. He just has more ammunition to push back against those critics.
Boston Red Sox CBO Craig Breslow Responds to Critics
It’s nice to be the one who gets the last laugh. For Craig Breslow, he certainly seems to feel that way now that the Red Sox have clinched a spot in the playoffs.
Boston didn’t clinch by winning, but by having other teams lose. So, after losing 5-1 to the Tampa Bay Rays on Sunday, the Red Sox partied in the Tropicana Field locker room. Among the players was Breslow himself, who shared a message publicly.
“Proud of the players,” Breslow said. “The staff. This has been a turbulent season, but, ultimately, we talked from the beginning of the offseason through Spring Training about putting together a team that we felt like was capable of getting to the postseason and a deep postseason run. This is certainly an accomplishment, but it’s not the primary objective here. So, we’ve still got a bunch of important games ahead of us.”
In April, Breslow fired manager Alex Cora and several other coaches. It was a massive move to shake up the staff, which was seen as an attempt to save himself at the time. Now, with the turnaround completed, it looks more successful than ever.
“I believed in the players that we had,” Breslow said. “And I felt it was really important that we acted definitively and decisively when we did, so that we could create an environment around the players that was supportive, that would allow them to thrive, and they responded. While there may have been some people that questioned what this group was capable of, I think they answered resoundingly.”
The Red Sox haven’t made the World Series since 2018. Since then, they’ve made the playoffs twice, in 2021 and 2025. In 2021, they made a run to the ALCS, while they were knocked out in the ALWCS last season. So, it’s been a while since they made a deep run.
The Red Sox are on a Collision Course with the Yankees
A season ago, the Red Sox ended up making the playoffs as a Wild Card team, before going to the Bronx to play the New York Yankees. They’d win Game 1, but couldn’t put the Yankees away in Game 2, and the bats never showed up for Game 3. It was a very quick exit for Boston.
Now, unless there’s a very surprising change in the next few days, the Red Sox are on a collision course to go to the Bronx to play the Yankees. They can’t afford to get quickly eliminated again.
Craig Breslow will be harshly judged if the Red Sox can’t beat the Yankees. Fair or not, that’s how it goes in Boston. The mid-season turnaround could be a distant memory in just a couple of weeks.

As the clinch celebration played out in the Tropicana Field visitors’ clubhouse early Sunday evening, the incompleteness of the moment was not lost on the revelling Boston Red Sox.
The achievement was dampened, and not only in the literal sense by the champagne with which the Red Sox doused each other and the room. That they had lost the series to the Tampa Bay Rays barely an hour earlier and instead had their ticket punched via an Atlanta Braves victory over the Houston Astros. The Red Sox are 9-9 this month, struggling offensively, without on several injured stars, and are their first postseason round will almost certainly be a rematch of last year’s best-of-three Wild Card series at Yankee Stadium, where they fell to their rivals 2-1.
In other words, there is much work to be done. The Red Sox know it, and they are eager to prove they did not come this far to only go this far.
“This has been a turbulent season,” Red Sox chief baseball officer Craig Breslow told reporters. “This is certainly an accomplishment, but it’s not the primary objective here.”
But neither the recent struggles nor the battles ahead should diminish the magnitude of the overall achievement of getting to this point.
The Red Sox lost American League Cy Young runner-up Garrett Crochet to a shoulder injury in mid-April, and he has yet to return.
They fired manager Alex Cora and several coaches in the middle of a late-April road series in Baltimore, and promoted Triple-A Worcester skipper Chad Tracy and several others from their minor league coaching ranks.
Injuries sidelined star outfielder Roman Anthony and veteran shortstop Trevor Story from early May until the very end of August.
The Red Sox owned their worst home record to start a season since 1932, and were 15 1/2 games out of first in the American League East in June.
On June 24, they fell to 14 games under .500. On Sunday, they became the fourth team in Major League Baseball history to go from as many as 14 games under .500 to the postseason in the same season.
“We needed time, and the time came for us,” veteran first baseman Willson Contreras told his teammates in the clubhouse. “I’m very proud of you all.”
“It’s 162 for a reason,” echoed third baseman Caleb Durbin.
“Obviously, getting where we want to go, but ultimately, what we had to overcome to get here makes it all the more sweet,” Tracy said. “We had a long way to go, and they never stopped, and they didn’t take no for an answer.”
This year looked lost, and the Red Sox managed to save it. They maintained an unshakeable belief in themselves, and it has already taken them to places most of the baseball world doubted it could go.
“Belief, belief, belief,” Contreras told reporters. “That was my main word, and that’s what I did from Day 1.”
The Red Sox are not a perfect team. But they certainly have the grit and gumption to go further than expected, as evidenced by the fact that they have already done so by reaching this point.
“We know how it felt when we left New York at the end of the year,” Story said. “You know how it made me feel. So that stayed with me.”
“They came together, and they found a way to get it done, and they had a long way to go to do it,” Tracy said. “They’re very battle-tested, and I’m super, super proud of them.”
“We don’t care where we play,” Tracy said. “You go back to July, and most people didn’t think we’d even be standing here. So it doesn’t matter where we play.”
“We’re in,” Tracy continued. “You got a ticket to the dance, and now you got to go take care of it there.”
“We’re in, baby,” Story said. “Let’s go.”
“Now, this is the moment,” right-fielder Wilyer Abreu said, “that we (were) waiting for.”

The Boston Red Sox are expected to have to pay up to keep a star pitcher beyond 2026. At the moment, Sonny Gray’s future in Beantown is very much in the air. The three-time All-Star is currently in his final year under contract. The two sides do, however, have a $30 million mutual option to extend his stay in Boston another year.
Despite this substantial salary, Gray would likely receive more money in the long term if he hit free agency. It was previously pointed out that the star would receive $10 million from the Red Sox if he declined the option. He could very well opt to collect the $10 million and then look for a lucrative multi-year deal elsewhere. If so, just how much money could the ace get in the winter?
Mass Live’s Chris Cotillo believes Gray could receive at least $75 million in the open market. “As a free agent, Gray’s renaissance season may position him to receive a lucrative deal that some in the industry expect to match or exceed the three-year, $75 million deal the Rangers gave to Nathan Eovaldi two winters ago,” writes Cotillo.
As the beat writer alludes to, Gray is experiencing a stellar campaign in his first season with the Boston Red Sox. The starter currently leads the American League with 17 wins and has posted a minuscule 2.82 ERA and 1.16 WHIP. Boston previously acquired the veteran in an offseason trade with the St. Louis Cardinals.
Boston Red Sox Hopeful Sonny Gray Returns to Team in 2027
While Gray could very well become a free agent, he has also recently admitted he is willing to return to the Boston Red Sox in 2027. As Cotillo reported, the pitcher claimed he was “definitely” open to signing an extension with the club. Craig Breslow, Boston’s president of baseball operations, will surely be looking to extend the star’s stay.
There is, however, a major wild card in all of this. Gray has recently hinted that he could very well retire soon. During a recent interview with The Boston Globe, the ace claimed that he would “be done in a heartbeat” if his family asked him to step away from the game.
Assuming the Boston Red Sox pitcher returns for his 15th MLB season and declines the mutual option, he should be positioned well in free agency, though. The upcoming starting pitching free agent class is not exactly super strong. Tarik Skubal is there, but Kevin Gausman and Freddy Peralta have seemingly hurt their values recently.
Boston Needs Star to Lead Team During Playoffs
For now, the Boston Red Sox will head towards the playoffs with Gray leading the way. Boston is currently in the fifth spot in the American League postseason standings. At the moment, they are projected to play against their bitter rivals, the New York Yankees, in the first round of the playoffs.
The veteran is likely to be the Boston Red Sox’s top starting pitcher during the upcoming postseason. The star leads the team’s rotation in wins, starts, innings, WAR, and ERA. He most recently allowed just three earned runs in six and a third innings during Boston’s victory on September 17.

We won't spend too long belaboring how bad the Kyle Harrison-Caleb Durbin looked for the Boston Red Sox after a few months; the southpaw had emerged as a genuine National League Cy Young contender for the Milwaukee Brewers in the first half, while the third baseman was one of the league's worst qualified hitters through the beginning of June. Tack on the fact that Shane Drohan has become a valuable starter in his own right this year while Andruw Monasterio has been worth negative fWAR, and you've got a recipe for an all-time disaster of a trade.
And yet, after the tide began shifting over the summer, we can now definitively say the pendulum has swung back in the other direction. Durbin has been a star since June 1, posting an .812 OPS and a 129 wRC+. Meanwhile, Harrison is struggling so badly that he's now been moved out of the Brewers' rotation entirely.
It's far too early to suggest that the Red Sox have made up that early gap and are now the winners of the blockbuster trade, but it's clear that their decision to go all-in for Durbin wasn't a foolish one.
Red Sox just need to break even now to win Caleb Durbin trade in the future
In that same post-June-1 span, Harrison has pitched to an 6.10 ERA and 5.38 FIP, allowing a whopping 17 home runs over just 59 innings. A bout with forearm tightness near the All-Star break definitely has something to do with his second-half collapse, but he hasn't been pitching like an ace for quite a while. The fact that there's been conversations about him being left off the Brewers' postseason roster entirely should tell you all you need to know about the southpaw's recent struggles.
Durbin is trending in the exact opposite direction, as he's currently the seventh-most valuable third baseman in the league by fWAR (2.9) this season. A lot of that has to do with how excellent his baserunning and glove have been, but saying that someone is above average in every phase of the game isn't exactly a bad thing. He's a couple of steals and some favorable votes away from a 20 SB, Gold Glove campaign in his Red Sox debut. Not too shabby, eh?
It's also worth factoring in the other players Craig Breslow pried out of Milwaukee; neither Monasterio nor Anthony Seigler have been great in limited duty in Boston, but the former has produced some timely hits while playing all four infield positions while the latter has a 102 wRC+ in just under 175 plate appearances this year.
Then there's Owen Hull, whom the Red Sox selected with the compensatory draft pick the Brewers forked over in the trade. All he did after being drafted was mash in High-A, posting a .967 OPS in 24 games.
With Durbin under contract through 2031 and Hull sure to fly up the prospect rankings over the offseason, there's a good chance that the Sox can win this trade down the road, so long as they continue to break even for now.

RedSoxRoundtable's Zach Coe discusses the potential relievers who could step up and fill the void left behind by Justin Slaten after it was revealed the right-hander was unlikely to return from the injured list in 2026. Be sure to join our FREE community over on RedSoxRoundtable.com!
After an incredible July that saw the Boston Red Sox go 21-4, ultimately saving their season and propelling them into postseason position, the team has given key contributors time on the injured list to address lingering injuries. Among the players placed on the IL was right-handed reliever Justin Slaten, who was dealing with right elbow soreness.
After initially expecting to miss the minimum of 15 days or somewhere close to it, the 29-year-old continued to experience soreness as he began throwing progressions, leading the team to shut him down each time. On Tuesday, interim manager Chad Tracy announced that Slaten received a PRP injection to treat "degenerative changes in his flexor mass," ending his season.
With Slaten set to miss the remainder of the year, the pressure is on these pitchers to help bridge the gap between the starter and All-Star closer Aroldis Chapman:
Tyron Guerrero
Guerrero was expected to be activated off the injured list ahead of Wednesday night's loss to the Texas Rangers, but tightness in his lower back led the team to delay his activation. Still, though, upon his activation, Guerrero will become one of the primary seventh-inning options for Tracy to turn to.
The 35-year-old flamethrower has been an incredible find for Chief Baseball Officer Craig Breslow, posting a 3.26 ERA in 38.2 innings in 2026. However, he hit a rough patch before landing on the IL, allowing eight earned runs in his last 13.2 innings. Boston will need him to return to the pitcher he was for the first 38.2 innings of his season, when he posted a 2.16 ERA.
After not allowing a single earned run in his first 10 appearances after being dealt to Boston at the trade deadline, the 28-year-old lefty has struggled in his last six outings, allowing five earned runs, including three in a blow-up appearance in Wednesday's loss.
Miller told reporters after the loss that he was working through a mechanical issue that led to the struggles. However, he is the primary left-handed high-leverage arm before Chapman, so the team will need him to get those issues squared away ahead of what's likely to be a Wild Card-round matchup against a New York Yankees lineup that's lefty-heavy.
No single pitcher has stepped up more for the Red Sox as they shuffled Garrett Whitlock, Slaten, and Guerrero on the injured list than Weissert. After a brief demotion to Triple-A Worcester on Aug. 7, Weissert returned to the big leagues on Aug. 13, taking Whitlock's spot on the active roster, and has been lights out ever since. In 10.2 innings since being recalled, the 31-year-old right-hander has allowed only two earned runs on 12 hits, striking out 14 and walking only four.
Weissert figures to be the leader in the clubhouse to take over Slaten's role in the bullpen.
A trio of injured options
The Red Sox have several pitchers looking to return from the injured list before the end of the regular season who could factor into the team's playoff push, including 2025 Cy Young Award runner-up Garrett Crochet, 2024 All-Star Tanner Houck, and Johan Oviedo.
Crochet
The 27-year-old ace has thrown four bullpen sessions since restarting a throwing progression on Aug. 3, with his most recent outing, a 30-pitch up-and-down session on the Fenway Park mound, coming on Tuesday afternoon. While Crochet, if healthy enough to appear in games, will almost certainly be on the postseason roster, he is expected to make multi-inning appearances rather than one-inning spurts like Slaten had been used, making him a valuable weapon but an imperfect replacement.
Houck
The now-30-year-old right-hander is attempting to return to the Boston staff in a "Swiss Army knife" role after undergoing Tommy John surgery in August 2025. Houck has already made three rehab appearances with both Double-A Portland and Triple-A Worcester, allowing two earned runs on one hit, walking four, and striking out seven in 4.2 innings. He is expected to return to Worcester on Saturday for a 40-50 pitch outing before potentially rejoining the Red Sox.
Though what exactly Houck can contribute after being out of major league action since May 2025 remains to be seen.
Oviedo
A bit of a forgotten man in the 2026 Red Sox season is the 28-year-old right-hander, who made only one appearance before landing on the injured list on April 3 with right elbow inflammation. Oviedo will make his first rehab appearance Thursday night with Worcester before deciding on next steps; at this point, the risk likely outweighs the reward of making the postseason roster.
Tracy, Breslow, and the rest of Boston's decision makers will have 10 games to make their final decisions on how exactly the postseason roster will look, and who will replace Slaten's high-leverage innings.
Up next for the Sox
The Red Sox will look to avoid the sweep at the hands of the Texas Rangers in Thursday's series finale from Globe Life Field. Sonny Gray (17-5, 2.76 ERA) gets the start for Boston opposite Tyler Alexander (5-2, 3.38 ERA) for Texas. First pitch is set for 8:05 p.m. ET.

When the Boston Red Sox sent former top-prospect Marcelo Mayer to the San Francisco Giants for Erik Miller, CBO Craig Breslow was sending a major signal. This season is about winning, and Miller will be more help with that now.
For a while, the hard-throwing lefty has been exactly that. A major spark out of the bullpen who makes the Red Sox incredibly intimidating on the mound in the late innings. In his first 14 appearances with Boston, Miller gave up just two runs.
The last two games have been more of a struggle for Miller, though. In 1.1 innings, he’s given up four runs. That includes three runs in Wednesday’s rough loss to the Texas Rangers, which was good enough for Miller to earn a loss.
Boston Red Sox RP Erik Miller Opened Up on Struggles
Following Wednesday’s loss, Erik Miller faced the media following the game. There, he explained that his main issue on Wednesday was that he had control issues. Those control issues put him in bad counts, which made him predictable.
“Just not doing what I’ve been doing well,” Erik Miller said. “Just not getting ahead of guys. Getting behind. Falling into hitters’ counts… Guy knows what’s coming, it usually doesn’t end well. Just kind of working through some stuff right now.”
Red Sox fans and media both noticed Miller saying that he’s working through some stuff. Luckily, that doesn’t mean an injury. It’s more a reference to letting his mechanics get away from him.
“Yeah. Some stuff I’m trying to clean up a little. At some point throughout the year, stuff crops up. You’ve been doing really well and some bad habits kind of come up. So, I’ve just got to work through it. Get back to what I was doing and go from there,” Miller said.
The Red Sox need the version of Miller they’ve largely gotten since the trade. He has a 2.87 ERA in Boston, to go along with a 1.277 WHIP and 14.9 strikeouts per nine. That’s in 15.2 innings over 16 appearances.
Garrett Crochet Will Return to the Red Sox as a Reliever
The Red Sox bullpen is set to get a major boost soon. Ace pitcher Garrett Crochet is getting ready to make his return, but it won’t be as a starter. It’ll be as another power lefty for the bullpen to use.
The expectation had been that Crochet won’t be able to make a rehab and would jump back in right as the first-round of the playoffs start. That may not be the case now. It was recently reported that he could be ready even sooner. That means he’ll potentially pitch in the regular season as a kind of rehab.
“The comebacks of potential October contributors like Tanner Houck, Garrett Crochet, Johan Oviedo and others might also be aided by the fact the Red Sox might have a week (or more) to set up for the postseason,” Chris Cotillo of MassLive wrote. “It’s not out of the question that the club has someone like Crochet pitch in one of the final regular season games of the year in what’s effectively a rehab outing at the major league level in a game that matters little in the standings.”
It’s excellent news for the Red Sox. With Aroldis Chapman, Garrett Whitlock, a healthy Garrett Crochet, and Erik Miller, Boston can feel very confident if they get just five innings from a starter.

Back in April, the Boston Red Sox's season was going off the rails.
The Red Sox started the season off with a 10-17 record and opted to fire a World Series-winning manager in Alex Cora — plus a handful of other coaches — and take a gamble by turning the reins over to interim manager Chad Tracy. At the time, it seemed like the sky was falling. That's because the losses kept piling up, so much so that the Red Sox were 14 games below .500 at 32-46 on June 25.
At the time, the season looked like a disaster. The Red Sox were trending towards being sellers ahead of the trade deadline, both Roman Anthony and Garrett Crochet were on the Injured List with no end in sight, and it seemed like chief baseball officer Craig Breslow's seat was getting hotter and hotter. But the Red Sox transformed their season and now, with the season winding down, ESPN's Buster Olney reported on Wednesday that the expectation is that both Breslow and Tracy will stay on with Boston beyond the 2026 season.
"But Breslow's vision of a team succeeding with pitching and defense fully manifested, and the Red Sox are closing in on a playoff berth and will likely face the Yankees in the wild-card round, again," Olney wrote. "Manager Chad Tracy has been working under an interim tag all season, something of a head-scratcher; it may be that the two sides talked about the idea of an extension in midseason but set aside the topic for the offseason. But Boston is now expected to retain both Breslow and Tracy."
The Red Sox Are Making The Right Call
This is undoubtedly the right call for the Red Sox at this time.
Let's start with Breslow. Whether you love him or not, he has built a team that can go on a run. Sure, there have been some misses over the last few years. Losing Alex Bregman was a public relations disaster. Not landing one of the big free agent bats, including Kyle Schwarber and Pete Alonso, this past offseason also was a surprise. But there are far more wins under Breslow's belt, than losses.
Sonny Gray is going to get Cy Young Award votes and has been Boston's ace this season. Ranger Suárez was an All-Star. Willson Contreras was an All-Star. Caleb Durbin is the heart and the soul of the 2026 Red Sox. Now, the Red Sox have an All-Star catcher on their hands in Adley Rutschman. Bringing back Mickey Gasper has turned into a game-changing move. And the list goes on. The Red Sox have a roster that can make noise.
On the Tracy front, there was obviously a learning curve to being a big league manager taking over during a season, especially in such a high-profile market, like Boston. He has handled the role with grace and has clearly gotten better as the year has gone on. Plus, it doesn't hurt that the Red Sox went on a historic 15-game winning streak and put together one of the best mid-season turnarounds in MLB history. All in all, these two should both be back in 2026 and it sounds like that will be the reality.

The Boston Red Sox are in the middle of a postseason push this September, but one the 2026 season comes to a close, there are going to be some huge questions the Red Sox will need to answer.
Whether it's about the future of Jarren Duran in the outfield, or how the team will handle the infield setup with Franklin Arias potentially an option, this is a very important offseason. But one of the keys to the offseason will revolve around Sonny Gray.
Tim Kelly of Bleacher Report highlighted the $30 million question the Red Sox will have with Gray this fall and winter. With a $30M mutual option, the Red Sox are at real risk of losing Gray to the open market this offseason.
Red Sox facing tricky $30M Sonny Gray problem
"Considering he'll pitch next season at 37, he's probably not going to get more than $30 million for 2027 as a free agent," Kelly writes. "However, if he declines the option, the Red Sox will owe him a $10 million buyout."
Boston is surely going to accept their side of the $30 million mutual option, considering how great Gray has been for the Red Sox this season.
But when it comes to whether Gray will accept the option or not, this $10 million buyout presents a big problem for the Red Sox.
It would not be a surprise if Gray declined the option, got the $10M buyout from the Red Sox, and then sought out a $20 million per-year contract.
Even though Gray is older, some team, whether it's the Red Sox or another club, will surely be willing to spend $20 million to land Gray.
But what makes it so tricky is that Gray could sign a two-year, $40 million deal on the open market, guaranteeing he lands an extra $20 million in 2028, regardless of his performance and health during the 2027 season.
He has a 2.76 ERA and a 17-5 record with the Red Sox in 2026, and is deserving of a big contract if he hits the open market. Even though he's older, his incredible 2026 season could present a challenge for the Red Sox.
Teams are going to have interest in Gray, and his $30 million option presents a big problem for the Red Sox. They could be out a key starter and lose some money in the process. This is a tricky situation, and one Craig Breslow needs to manage well.

When the Boston Red Sox made some additions to their starting rotation last winter, they were hoping to rebuild it around ace Garrett Crochet. Little did they know that making those moves would turn out to be monster moves.
After losing out on Alex Bregman in free agency to the Chicago Cubs, Chief Baseball Officer Craig Breslow pivoted to pitching. He signed left-hander Ranger Suárez of the Philadelphia Phillies. Earlier in the offseason, Breslow acquired veteran Sonny Gray from the St. Louis Cardinals.
That is turning into the biggest offseason addition made by Boston. He is going to finish at least in the top 5 in the American League Cy Young voting, but will be a free agent following the season with an option for 2027. Breslow and Gray will have a decision to make this winter, according to Kerry Miller of Bleacher Report.
Boston Red Sox Facing Sonny Gray Decision This Winter
When decisions are to be made for 2027, Gray has a mutual option of $30 million. Now, whether or not Gray plays next season remains to be seen, according to Alex Speier of the Boston Globe.
“If my family wants me to hang it up, I’ll be done in a heartbeat,” Gray said, per Speier.
If they don’t want him to retire, the Red Sox would love to have him back. He is 17-5 in his first season in Boston with a 2.76 ERA in 27 starts. He has been a workhorse in 156.2 innings with 140 strikeouts. Gray has struggled in recent outings. However, he is still on track to get the ball in Game 1 of the AL wild-card series.
“Even with major money committed to Ranger Suárez and Garrett Crochet in the rotation already, chief baseball officer Craig Breslow will probably pick up the team’s half of the option,” Miller wrote.
“The question is whether Gray will. Considering he’ll pitch next season at 37, he’s probably not going to get more than $30 million for 2027 as a free agent. However, if he declines the option, the Red Sox will owe him a $10 million buyout. So he could collect that buyout, try to get at least $20 million for 2027, and perhaps pursue a multi-year commitment. He has plenty to consider.”
Crochet has been out injured for a majority of this season and is looking for a postseason return. Suárez has been better in his last couple of starts in September.
Boston Red Sox Facing Key Offseason Decision
Gray is scheduled to make his next start on Thursday night against the Texas Rangers in Arlington. Then he’ll get one more next week before his start in the wild-card round. Depending on how far the Red Sox go, all eyes could turn to 2027.
Boston’s rotation next season, if healthy when the season begins, with Gray, could be one of the top ones in the American League. If there is any question as to whether or not Gray has another year left in him, that should have been answered by his 2026 season.
There are some big decisions coming for Breslow this winter. Gray is going to be at the top of that list.

When Boston was at its lowest, Craig Breslow's position as chief baseball officer was in question.
Now, ESPN's Buster Olney reports that the Red Sox are expected to sign Tracy as the club's full-time manager. In addition, Breslow is likely to remain with the organization.
"Manager Chad Tracy has been working under an interim tag all season, something of a head-scratcher; it may be that the two sides talked about the idea of an extension in midseason but set aside the topic for the offseason," Olney wrote Wednesday. Before he was named interim manager in the Majors, Tracy was the manager of Boston's Triple-A affiliate, the Worcester Red Sox.
He is the son of former MLB manager Jim Tracy, who spent time with the Los Angeles Dodgers (2001-05), Pittsburgh Pirates (2006-07), and Colorado Rockies (2009-12).
It appears the Red Sox feel like Tracy is the right man for the job. Perhaps they are waiting until after the season for the 41-year-old to sign an extension.

Chad Tracy helped the Boston Red Sox change their entire season.
Boston seemed like a goner when it emptied out its coaching staff early in the year and moved Tracy up from Triple-A Worcester to be the interim manager at the MLB level.
But now in mid-September, the Red Sox are holding onto a playoff spot and will likely finish strong enough to indeed go to the postseason.
Tracy, to whatever extent you believe a manager should get credit for such things, has been at the heart of it.
The Red Sox went on a 15-game winning streak with Tracy at the helm, tying a franchise record for wins in a row. And they’ve stayed relatively strong since then, too.
The main intrigue surrounding Tracy, though, has been the interim tag. Boston could’ve probably removed the “interim manager” label at some point, but that hasn’t happened.
It at least leaves the door open for what might happen in Tracy’s future. Would there be a world where he doesn’t return next season?
It’s certainly looking like he’ll be back.
MLB Insider on Chad Tracy
ESPN’s Buster Olney wrote a new article on Wednesday in which he examined a number of managerial decisions, including Tracy.
Olney suggests that Tracy isn’t going anywhere.
“Manager Chad Tracy has been working under an interim tag all season, something of a head-scratcher; it may be that the two sides talked about the idea of an extension in midseason but set aside the topic for the offseason,” Olney writes. “But Boston is now expected to retain both (Craig) Breslow and Tracy.”
Tracy is a former MLB player who has a lot of good relationships in the Boston organization after first managing in the minor leagues.
It may not have been the plan for the Red Sox that he does so well that he gets kept around for a long time. He was just a safe choice at the time of the interim hiring.
It has simply worked out better than anyone could’ve possibly imagined, and the Red Sox can’t run from that now.
Craig Breslow’s Future
When the Red Sox were scuffling, the fate of front office decision maker Craig Breslow seemed sealed.
But now that they’ve turned it around, as Olney mentions above, Breslow’s job seems safe, too.
“In mid-June, the growing perspective within some corners of the Boston organization was that the team would move on from Craig Breslow as the head of baseball operations,” Olney writes. “But Breslow’s vision of a team succeeding with pitching and defense fully manifested, and the Red Sox are closing in on a playoff berth and will likely face the Yankees in the wild-card round, again.”
Breslow has the odd front office background of being a former relief pitcher, but right now, it seems that his strategy has worked, and it’s the results that matter.

Heading into the playoffs, the Boston Red Sox have one of the best bullpens in all of baseball. A major reason why is the dominance of setup man Garrett Whitlock.
At one point, Whitlock was a pitcher who the Red Sox had hoped to make into a starter. His body, seemingly, couldn’t handle the workload, though. So, he moved to the bullpen where he’s been dominant. Still, there is a willingness that Whitlock recently shared with The Boston Globe to return to the rotation.
“I definitely know my body better and know everything better now, and so it’s definitely something I’d be open to. Will I?” Whitlock said. “I’m not going to walk into [chief baseball officer Craig Breslow’s] office and be like, ‘Hey, I’m starting.’ So it’s one of those things where the team would have to be on board with it and just talk through everything and go through it. But it’s something I’d always be open to.”
It’s been since 2024 when Whitlock last started for the Red Sox. Since then, he’s become one of the game’s elite relievers. In 2026 alone, he has a 1.81 ERA, a 0.826 WHIP, and 10.5 strikeouts per nine in 49.2 innings of work.
“I doubt Boston will do it. We’re pretty good on starting depth,” Whitlock said. “If I become a free agent and a team approaches me about it, I’m open to it and see how it goes.”
Whitlock is a different pitcher now than he was when he was starting games. He’s a sinker pitcher now, and he’s ditched his fastball. He’s also changed his changeup grip, making it one of the best pitches in MLB.
Seth Lugo of the Kansas City Royals recently made a similar switch back and forth. As he explained it, the switch back to starting is actually easier.
“Once you make the switch back, you have the confidence. The problems you had earlier in your career, [which] sent you to the ’pen in the first place — you’re aware why those mistakes happened,” Lugo said.
Injuries Have Plagued Garrett Whitlock With the Boston Red Sox
The major reason why the Red Sox sent Garrett Whitlock to the bullpen was that his body wasn’t holding up to the workload. Injuries became a major issue at that point in his career.
Among the injuries Whitlock has battled in his career are a right pec strain, right hip inflammation, right hip impingement, right elbow ulnar neuritis, right elbow inflammation again, and in 2024 he would finally need an internal brace to repair a torn UCL. It was an alternative to Tommy John. Even in 2026, as a reliever, Whitlock landed on the IL with a left leg strain.
Still, he’s stayed healthier in the bullpen overall. So, it’s made sense to keep him there.
Whitlock isn’t the only starter forced into the bullpen over the years. He’s even fairly close with a couple of them from his time on Team USA in the World Baseball Classic. They’re even able to joke about that role now.
“We all joke that we’re all failed starters,” Whitlock said.
Whitlock’s Contract Situation With the Red Sox
In April of 2022, the Red Sox extended Garrett Whitlock. He’s currently on a four-year, $18.75 million deal. That’s going to expire at the end of the season, though there are club options for the next two seasons.
When the Red Sox signed that extension, Whitlock was a starting pitcher. Now a relief pitcher, the value of the deal does change a little bit. His 2027 option is worth $8.25 million and the 2028 option is worth $10.5 million.
The Red Sox certainly don’t want to see Whitlock walk. The 30 year old has, undeniably, been elite for them. So, they are going to need to consider their options. That is, to pick up those options, extend Whitlock again, or let him walk in free agency. Making that a tougher decision are the upcoming CBA negotiations.
Notably, even Whitlock’s 2028 option would be outside the current top 10 in AAV for the 2026 season among relievers. So, for his production, the Red Sox are getting great value.

The Boston Red Sox never fully resolved their outfield-designated hitter logjam, and once again it may create a roster conundrum. For much of the season, things had worked themselves out one way or another.
Spending most of the season without Roman Anthony certainly wasn't ideal, but it did make for a cleaner lineup card. His return, of course, has been music to our ears, and it saved the Red Sox from another tough roster decision due to the injuries to Masataka Yoshida and Ceddanne Rafaela.
There's a point where push might come to shove, though, and Boston is forced to make a tough choice. Chad Tracy won't rule out Yoshida returning in time for the playoffs, which would lead to some interesting decisions.
"He's [Yoshida] not on the 60-day (injured list). It's just a matter of how does he heal over the next handful of weeks," the interim skipper said.
If the 33-year-old can return in time for October, it could put the likes of Mickey Gasper or Nick Sogard in the crosshairs. At which point, the Red Sox will have to make a choice and leave someone unhappy.
Masataka Yoshida shouldn't cost Mickey Gasper or Nick Sogard a spot on the Red Sox playoff roster
Just because Yoshida can come back (and that's still up in the air) doesn't mean he should. The NPB veteran has done what he's always done since coming stateside, hit for some average and get on base, but has provided very little in the power department.
Through 87 games, he's hit .274/.347/.399 with five homers, which is nothing to sneeze at, but doesn't really scratch the Red Sox's power itch. On top of that, despite what we saw in the World Baseball Classic, he has little defensive value and will be a nonfactor in the outfield coming off a serious hamstring strain.
Comparatively, Gasper's hot bat better fits what Boston needs. While he might simply be riding the wave rather than emerging as a true offensive force, the switch-hitter has brought the pop with eight dingers in just 187 plate appearances and a .500 slugging percentage, all while providing similar contact and on-base numbers to Yoshida.
Furthermore, he has some value in the field with the ability to fill in behind the plate if needed, as well as play first base. That alone gives him an edge over the DH-only Yoshida.
As for Sogard, his offensive profile is similar to Yoshida's, but his positional versatility is far superior. Depending on Curtis Mead's recovery, Sogard is a valuable insurance policy at second base that should have him over Yoshida in the October pecking order, too.
Craig Breslow's failure to move Jarren Duran before he became a radioactive asset is the real key here. Not only does it represent a missed opportunity for the Red Sox, but it is also the main barrier for Yoshida, given that Boston can't really afford to carry a DH-only player. With that, the choice should be clear. Even if Yoshida is healthy, he needs to sit this October out.

But deep down inside, in a maybe-one-day-eventually sort of way, Garrett Whitlock harbors aspirations to try again to be a starting pitcher, to return to the rotation.

“I definitely know my body better and know everything better now, and so it’s definitely something I’d be open to. Will I?” Whitlock said. “I’m not going to walk into [chief baseball officer Craig Breslow’s] office and be like, ‘Hey, I’m starting.’ So it’s one of those things where the team would have to be on board with it and just talk through everything and go through it. But it’s something I’d always be open to.”
Whitlock is intrigued enough to have picked the brain in recent months of Griffin Jax, the righthander whom the Rays converted from reliever to starter this season.
Jax, 31, had an 8.00 ERA in 11 relief appearances, moved to the rotation in April, slowly built up his pitch count, and has a 3.59 ERA in 20 starts.
Whitlock and Jax became buddies when they played together for Team USA during the World Baseball Classic in March. They’ve texted about what amounts to an experiment for Jax.
Jax’s take, per Whitlock: Everything he learned in his years as a reliever, several as a high-end reliever, made him a better pitcher, regardless of role. Tweaks to his repertoire, knowing how to attack hitters, and ensuring his body recovers between outings — it all applies to being a starter.
Whitlock has had similar conversations with the Cubs’ Clay Holmes, another Team USA teammate. He made the switch last year.
“We all joke that we’re all failed starters,” Whitlock said of his bullpen brethren.
Take it from the Royals’ Seth Lugo, who beat the Red Sox on Friday.
He and Whitlock have had very similar career arcs: They reached the majors in their mid-20s as non-elite prospects, bounced between the bullpen and rotation based on team need and their performance, and accepted their club wanting them in a relief role. They were excellent at it.
All along, Lugo, a consummate pro and good employee in his years as a Mets reliever, said he wanted to give starting another go — someday. Now, he is in his fourth season and third contract since getting the chance — once he became a free agent — and turning it into a successful and lucrative second act.
“It’s not as daunting as it seems,” Lugo said at Fenway Park over the weekend. “What happens is you first get to the big leagues and you try to be someone that you’re not, just from other influences, other recommendations. But you [learn] how to get guys out [as a reliever].
“Once you make the switch back, you have the confidence. The problems you had earlier in your career, [which] sent you to the ’pen in the first place — you’re aware why those mistakes happened.”
Lugo, like Whitlock, was a late-innings arm. He faced the other team’s best hitters in some of the most important moments of the game.
“Once you have success pitching the seventh, eighth, ninth inning, the first six innings become a lot easier,” he said. “As a reliever, when you’re going into a game, you’re a lot more stressed out than you are as a starter. So you start to recognize what you’re good at, how you can get out of those situations.”
Whitlock, who possesses a 1.81 ERA in 51 relief appearances this year, last made more than a handful of starts in 2023. Since then, he ditched the four-seam fastball to lean even more on his sinker, went with a slider instead of a sweeper, and changed his changeup, which has become highly effective.
In discussing the possibility, Whitlock is a realist: The Sox’ rotation seems full for the foreseeable future.
His contract includes team options for 2027 ($8.25 million) and 2028 ($10.5 million). Those are good deals for an elite reliever — and a really good deal for even a serviceable starter.
“I doubt Boston will do it. We’re pretty good on starting depth,” Whitlock said. “If I become a free agent and a team approaches me about it, I’m open to it and see how it goes.”
Perez on Abreu
Royals icon and Venezuela captain Salvador Perez, witness to Wilyer Abreu’s WBC star turn, is a big fan — and a big believer of Abreu on a big stage. “He’s going to be the MVP if Boston makes it to the World Series,” Perez said. “He’s built for a moment like that.” … Early returns on Adley Rutschman’s cortisone shot last week, intended to alleviate pain in his right elbow, are solid. Against Kansas City, he went 3 for 10 with a double, as many walks as strikeouts (two) — and played three games in a row for the first time since getting hurt. “It definitely helped a lot,” interim manager Chad Tracy said. “You can tell his body language and stuff too, he looks and feels pretty good.” … Garrett Crochet’s bullpen session Tuesday is scheduled for 30 pitches across two simulated innings, a step up from previous shorter sessions.

Andrew Bailey, Craig Breslow, and Kurt Suzuki were teammates with the Oakland Athletics from 2009-11. Now Bailey is the Red Sox pitching coach, Breslow is chief baseball officer, and Suzuki is managing the Angels.
Suzuki, a former catcher, knows the Red Sox pitching coach and chief baseball officer well. Bailey was a two-time All-Star closer with the Athletics, and Breslow made 202 appearances as a setup man during that time.
“I thought Bres would cure cancer when he was finished with baseball,” said Suzuki, referencing the lefthander graduating from Yale with a degree in molecular biophysics and biochemistry. “But I can see why he stayed in baseball. He was always ahead of the times the way he thought about the game.
“When I caught him, I called him ‘Everyday Bres.’ He was always ready to pitch every day, never complained, and always got people out. He was a good person to be around.”
Suzuki is not surprised to see his former teammates still involved in the game.
“I think we all love the game. We all had an interest to stay in the game beyond our playing time,” he said. “Bres pitched in the big leagues for a long time and gained a lot of information. I don’t know if I would have predicted he’d be running a team, but I’m not surprised.
“The same with [Bailey]. You knew he would have a bright future in the game if that was what he wanted. He’s one of the best pitching coaches around.”
A few other observations on the Red Sox:
▪ It seems funny to think about now, but Aroldis Chapman came to spring training in 2025 with no guarantee he would be the closer.
The lefthander was competing with Liam Hendriks, who was returning from Tommy John surgery. Breslow said at the time Justin Slaten also would receive consideration.
Chapman had 14 saves for the Pirates in 2024, but nine of them came in September for a last-place team.
Hendriks never had a save for the Sox. Slaten had one in March and two in April that season, and none since.
Chapman has converted 65 of 69 save opportunities for the Sox and taken steps that could lead to the Hall of Fame.
▪ No Red Sox infielder has won a Gold Glove since Ian Kinsler in 2018, and he joined the team at the trade deadline that season and started only 35 games at second base. For a full season, you have to go back to Pedroia in 2014.
Caleb Durbin is set to break that drought.
The third baseman has 11 defensive runs saved, the most in the American League by a wide margin. Tampa Bay’s Junior Caminero, with three, is a distant second. Durbin also leads in other metrics, including outs above average.
▪ As the season winds down, Wilyer Abreu is first in doubles, second in runs and home runs, fourth in RBIs, and fifth in OPS among AL outfielders.
The right fielder believes playing in the World Baseball Classic contributed significantly to that success.
“I worked a lot in the offseason to be prepared for the WBC,” Abreu said. “So when the season started, I was ready to go. That helped me a lot.”
Abreu also benefited from being around Venezuela hitting coach Miguel Cabrera and assistant manager Victor Martinez.
“I talked a lot to them about my approach and how to attack pitchers on what they throw,” he said. “Miggy was such a smart hitter, and he really helped me.”
▪ Fred Lynn was at Fenway Park for the Angels series this past week. He follows the Sox closely and often arrives at the park early to watch batting practice.
Most of the players had no idea who the 74-year-old guy with the good tan was, but Roman Anthony did and had a conversation on the field with Lynn on Tuesday.
“He was somebody I’d wanted to meet for a while, obviously. A legend,” Anthony said. “Somebody said he was out there, so I immediately wanted to say hello to him and his wife, and they were great.
“He shared some of his experiences here, his experiences when he left here. It was great to hear it.”
No. 19 talking to No. 19 was interesting to watch from a distance. Anthony received a lot of attention when he was called up last year, but nothing like the mania for Lynn and Jim Rice in 1975.
Anthony has looked up the statistics. He gets it.
“I got familiar with him when I got 19 when I first came up last year,” he said. “He was pretty excited about it and sent some love. Obviously, he was an unbelievable player, an unbelievable Red Sox. But a great human, too. It was awesome to interact with him.”
▪ The Sox traded for Curtis Mead on July 26. He started at second base against the Athletics in Sacramento the next day, and broke his left wrist when he was hit by a pitch in his second plate appearance.
Red Sox second basemen have since hit .245 with a .718 OPS and 21 RBIs. It’s not great, but nine American League teams have a lower OPS from their second basemen in that span, and 10 have a lower wRC+.
As for Mead, he is playing catch but isn’t hitting yet. The Sox haven’t ruled him out for the rest of the season, but interim manager Chad Tracy has acknowledged it’s unlikely Mead will return until 2027.
Connelly Early, who was traded for Mead, has yet to pitch for the Nationals because of an elbow injury. He is scheduled to make a rehab start for Double-A Harrisburg on Sunday. The Nationals hope he’ll be able to get into a major league game before the season ends.
▪ Baseball lost a legend last week when Joe McDonald passed away at the age of 97.
McDonald started in baseball in the 1940s working with the ticket takers at Ebbets Field. He joined the Mets in 1962 and became their general manager from 1975-80.
He later became GM of the Cardinals (1982-84) and Tigers (1991-92) before scouting for the Angels and Rockies. He finished his career scouting for the Red Sox from 2004-19.
“Joe was a joy to work with and always very generous in sharing his experience and expertise. He loved the game, was willing to go scout a player anywhere at any time, and just wanted to contribute,” said former Sox GM and current Fenway Sports Group senior adviser Theo Epstein, who hired McDonald. “Having two great former GMs like Joe and Bill Lajoie around was incredibly valuable to me. He will be missed.”
